prs.title: fix(client): drop sampling params for the Claude 5 generation and Haiku 5.5
prs.body:
## What

`anthropic_model_rejects_sampling` gates `temperature`/`top_p` out of Anthropic Messages bodies. The gate only knew `opus-4-7`, `opus-4-8`, `fable`, and `mythos`. Every model released after Opus 4.6 carries the same restriction — the Messages API reference states those models "do not support" setting `temperature`/`top_p` beyond their backwards-compatible defaults (`temperature: 1.0`, `top_p >= 0.99`), and the migration guides restate it per family: "Setting `temperature`, `top_p`, or `top_k` to any non-default value on Claude Opus 4.7 and later models, including Claude Opus 5.5, returns a 400 error". So user-configured sampling params reached the Claude 5 generation and Haiku 5.5 and returned a 400.

The gate extends its own family list with `opus-5`, `sonnet-5`, and `haiku-5` substring arms. Dropping the params entirely is always safe; sending a forbidden one bricks the request. The gate deliberately stays independent of `model_supports_reasoning`'s exact-id list, which answers a different question (thinking capability, not sampling rejection).

Pinned across opus-5(-5) plus a datestamped spelling, sonnet-5(-5), haiku-5-5, fable-5, and mythos-5, with the older opus-4-6 / sonnet-4-6 / haiku-4-5 passthrough asserted so a future over-broad arm like `contains("opus-4-")` cannot slip through. Docs re-checked 2026-10-08.

## Tests

- Extended `body_drops_sampling_params_for_models_that_reject_them`: the eight Claude-5/Haiku-5.5/Fable/Mythos spellings must omit both params; older models keep temperature (or top_p when alone).
- `cargo test -p codewhale-tui --lib body_drops_sampling` green; clippy `-D warnings` clean (lib).

Ported from the Pinvou/CodeWhale fork (#93, commit 3118c36b8); the Gemini and DeepSeek hunks of that fork commit are already covered upstream and are not included.

No-Issue: the heuristic Anthropic sampling gate missed Claude 5 / Haiku 5.5 on routes without exact catalog facts (port of fork PR #93)

prs.title: fix(compaction): scope legacy checkpoint recognition by era
prs.body:
## What

The restore lane already prefers the provenance-stamped compaction carrier, but the recompaction family still ran the loose predicate, which matches any user turn whose text merely starts with a legacy summary header. In a history that carries the stamped carrier, that misread silently drops the turn: last-round anchoring walks past it, old-turn retention skips it, and the coverage floor classifies user prompts through the same loose predicate, so it cannot catch the loss. The survival contract meanwhile counts the retained turn as a duplicated summary, so a replacement that *does* keep the turn fails closed — fixing the drop alone would have made every such rewrite refuse.

Checkpoint recognition in the recompaction family is now era-scoped through `history_is_post_provenance`:

- A history that contains a stamped carrier recognizes only stamped carriers as checkpoints. A pasted bare-header turn anchors the round, is retained verbatim, and does not count as a duplicated summary.
- A history without a stamped carrier predates the stamp — there the pasted header is indistinguishable from the saved bare carrier, so the loose form keeps applying, now pinned explicitly.
- The receipt count reads the replacement in its own era, except that a post-provenance **original** raises the bar to a stamped carrier: the engine stamps every replacement it builds, and the stamp is the only form request rewriting relocates, so a stampless replacement of a modern history is a dropped receipt even where a retained pasted turn would loosely count as one.
- Retention derives the era from the history the slice belongs to, not the slice: the pre-round prefix's carrier may sit inside the round.
- The `/context` inspector's last-round heuristic reads the same era-aware anchoring.

`validate_survival_contract.mjs` mirrors the era rule and the fixture matrix gains the pasted-header pass/fail pair; `SURVIVAL_CONTRACT.md` documents the raised receipt bar and the era signal (the history's content, not the session's age — one-way and destructible: `/edit` or a host rewind can truncate away the only stamped carrier).

## Tests

- `pasted_legacy_header_turn_is_content_in_a_post_provenance_history` — the pasted turn anchors the round, is retained verbatim, a replacement keeping it validates with exactly one receipt, and dropping it fails the coverage floor.
- `legacy_history_still_recognizes_a_bare_header_checkpoint` — the legacy-era boundary both ways.
- Two fixture-matrix cases (`pasted-legacy-header-survives-post-provenance` pass / `-dropped-` fail) run through both the Rust enforcement and the mjs validator (16 fixtures green).
- `cargo test -p codewhale-tui --lib compaction` 186 passed / 0 failed; clippy `-D warnings` clean (lib).

Ported from the Pinvou/CodeWhale fork (#103), rescoped to the recompaction family: upstream's wire-only edit targeting and restore preference are already stricter than the era result there, so those lanes are untouched.

No-Issue: recompaction dropped a pasted legacy-header user turn in a history with a stamped checkpoint (port of fork PR #103)

prs.title: fix(kimi): repair empty items schemas instead of dropping the tool
prs.body:
## What

Moonshot's MFJS schema validation fails any empty schema node with `MissingType`, and `sanitize_moonshot_chat_tools` answers by silently excluding the whole tool from the request. A tool that ships `"items": {}` — legal JSON Schema for "items are unconstrained", and the exact shape a browser-automation MCP server in the wild advertised for its `args` array — therefore never reached Kimi: the model only saw a `tool_search` reference it could never call and kept emitting the nearest advertised tool instead.

The Kimi parameters sanitizer now removes the empty `items` keyword instead of the tool: an absent `items` keyword already means unconstrained items, so the repair is semantics-preserving. Untyped nodes without a semantics-preserving MFJS equivalent (e.g. `{"items": {"description": "..."}}`) still fail closed with `MissingType`.

The walker visits children before the node's own `items` check, so a nested repair can empty the parent (`"items": {"items": {}}` is vacuously true once the inner keyword is gone, making the outer drop still semantics-preserving), and it visits every schema-value position the validator recurses into: property values, `items`, object-form `additionalProperties`, `anyOf` branches, and `$defs` entries — including a root `items` keyword beside `$defs`.

## Tests

- `kimi_parameters_repairs_empty_items_as_unconstrained` — the wild-found shape, nested occurrences, and the still-fail-closed described-only node.
- `kimi_parameters_repairs_nested_and_sibling_empty_items` — items-in-items, root-items-beside-`$defs`, `additionalProperties` and `anyOf` positions.
- `cargo test -p codewhale-tui --lib schema_sanitize` 63 passed / 0 failed; clippy `-D warnings` clean (lib).

Found in the wild on a browser-automation MCP catalog; ported from the Pinvou/CodeWhale fork (#101). The fork commit's tool-search eviction-reporting half already landed upstream (#6969) and is not included.

No-Issue: Moonshot dropped any tool whose schema has an empty `items` (port of fork PR #101)

prs.title: ci(sync): skip the CNB mirror when its token secret is absent
prs.body:
## What

`sync` fails on every push to a mirrored branch when the `CNB_GIT_TOKEN` repository secret is absent: "CNB_GIT_TOKEN secret is not set; cannot push to CNB." That is a repository-secret state, not a property of the commit — forks can never inherit the secret, so they report a red check no contributor can fix.

A `credentials` gate job probes the secret and skips the push when it is absent, emitting a notice that names the missing secret. Configured repositories keep the previous behavior, including the existing hard failure inside the push step, which still covers a caller pinned to an older revision of this workflow plus the window where the secret is deleted between the gate's probe and the push step.

`docs/CNB_MIRROR.md` documents the skip path and distinguishes "skipped because absent or misspelled" from "failed because expired" in the rotation section.

## Tests

- Workflow-parse level: jobs `credentials` + `sync`, `sync.if = needs.credentials.outputs.configured == 'true'` (verified locally; CI exercises the rest).
- The skip path is exercised by forks of the repository, where the secret cannot exist.

Co-authored with @zhuowp (original patch in the Pinvou/CodeWhale fork, #64); adapted to this workflow's retry/concurrency/`workflow_call` plumbing.

No-Issue: CI-only; forks cannot inherit CNB_GIT_TOKEN, so Sync to CNB fails on every fork push

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

When the tts tool is invoked during a conversation turn on Telegram, the system delivers two duplicate messages simultaneously:

A Voice Message with the synthesized audio AND the full turn reply text attached as its caption.
A Standalone Text Message (sendMessage) containing the exact same text content duplicated.

This leads to redundant text delivery where the user receives the same response twice (once as the voice note caption, once as a separate text bubble).

### Steps to reproduce

Configure Telegram channel and Microsoft / Edge TTS provider in openclaw.json.
Disable Auto-TTS (tts.auto: off).
Send a user prompt requesting voice output (e.g. "Please respond with voice" or "Generate a voice response").
The agent triggers the tts tool with speech text and completes the turn with closing text in <final>.
Observe the Telegram chat output.

### Expected behavior

The agent should either:

Deliver only the Voice Note (with or without caption), suppressing the subsequent redundant text sendMessage; OR
Deliver the Voice Note as audio and only send supplementary text if explicitly required, without repeating the exact same text twice.

### Actual behavior

The user receives two consecutive bubbles in Telegram at the exact same timestamp:

Bubble 1: Voice audio player + full text response as caption.
Bubble 2: Standalone text message with identical full text response.

### OpenClaw version

2026.9.3 (1391f7c) (upgraded from 2026.9.1)

### Operating system

Rocky Linux 10.1 x86_64

### Install method

_No response_

### Model

google/gemini-3.7-flash

### Provider / routing chain

Primary: google/gemini-3.7-flash (direct, no proxy) Fallbacks: disabled (user model override active for this session) TTS Provider: Microsoft Edge TTS (via talk-voice plugin)

### Additional provider/model setup details

_No response_

### Logs

```shell
Physical Evidence & Diagnostic Traces
1. Gateway Runtime Logs (~/.openclaw/logs/gateway.log)
log
2026-09-10T19:14:32.898+08:00 [telegram] Inbound message telegram:chatId=<redacted> -> @<bot> (messageId: 48084)
2026-09-10T19:14:37.190+08:00 [auto-reply/agent-turn-timing] milestone=tool_execution_started (calling tts)
2026-09-10T19:14:51.014+08:00 [telegram] outbound send ok accountId=default chatId=chatId=<redacted> messageId=48086 operation=sendMessage deliveryKind=text chunkCount=1
2. Media Store Artifacts (~/.openclaw/media/tool-speech-synthesis/)
-rw-r--r--. 1 user user 74736 2026-09-10 19:14:42 voice---31d8048c-c55e-4338-bb8c-b7a12634ecbe.mp3
3. Session History Trace

The turn transcript confirms that tts tool auto-delivered the audio payload with caption, but the pipeline subsequently dispatched the assistant's <final> text block through the standard text reply dispatcher without deduplication
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

- **Affected**: Any Telegram user invoking the explicit `tts` tool with Auto-TTS disabled on OpenClaw 2026.9.3.
- **Severity**: Annoying but does not block workflow. No data loss or security risk.
- **Frequency**: Always reproducible — every explicit `tts` tool call results in double delivery.
- **Consequence**: User receives duplicate messages on every voice response — one voice note with caption, one redundant standalone text bubble. Increases message noise and may confuse users expecting a single reply. No missed messages or extra provider cost observed.

### Additional information

- Initially suspected as a 2026.9.3 regression, but confirmed present in 2026.9.1 as well.
- This appears to be a long-standing issue rather than a regression.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

A first sessions_send to a freshly spawned acpx session changes its stored runtime metadata from ACP/session-key to implicit native and fails with ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Enable `@openclaw/acpx`.
2. Register a durable agent entry:
```json
{"runtime":{"type":"acp","acp":{"agent":"codex","backend":"acpx","mode":"persistent"}},"model":{"primary":"openai/gpt-5.6"}}
```
3. Spawn a persistent session through `/acp spawn codexacp --mode persistent --thread auto`.
4. Confirm with `sessions list --json` that the new row has `acpRuntime: true` and `agentRuntime: { id: "acpx", source: "session-key" }`.
5. Without restarting the gateway, call `sessions_send` with that session key, a short message, and `timeoutSeconds: 120`.
6. Inspect the same row again with `sessions list --json`.

Also reproduced with a non-colliding `claudeacp` entry.

### Expected behavior

`sessions_send` should deliver to the running ACP session and preserve `acpRuntime: true` and `agentRuntime.source: "session-key"`.

### Actual behavior

The send returns `ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED` with `sentBeforeError: true`. Immediately afterward, the same session row reports `acpRuntime: false` and `agentRuntime: { id: "codex", source: "implicit" }`.

### OpenClaw version

2026.9.3 (1391f7c)

### Operating system

Ubuntu Linux, Docker container

### Install method

Docker Compose; ghcr.io/openclaw/openclaw:latest

### Model

openai/gpt-5.6 (Codex); Claude Code subscription harness also reproduced

### Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw gateway -> @openclaw/acpx -> Codex CLI or Claude Code ACP harness

### Additional provider/model setup details

Codex CLI 0.153.4. Claude Code 2.1.267 with bundled `@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp`. Provider credentials are valid; inbound wake-and-reply was separately observed for both harnesses. No credentials are included here.

### Logs

```shell
Before send:

acpRuntime: true
agentRuntime: { id: "acpx", source: "session-key" }


Send result:

status: error
error: "ACP metadata is missing for <sessionKey>. Recreate this ACP session with /acp spawn and rebind the thread. | ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED"
sentBeforeError: true


After send:

acpRuntime: false
agentRuntime: { id: "codex", source: "implicit" }
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Sanitized session UUIDs are omitted. Gateway start time was unchanged across the reproduction, confirming no gateway restart between the valid ACP record and the failed send.

### Impact and severity

Affected: persistent ACP sessions using acpx, reproduced with both Codex and Claude harnesses. Severity: blocks ACP-agent-originated and direct session messaging after the metadata is overwritten. Frequency: reproduced on the first send for fresh sessions. Consequence: the session must be recreated and cannot be used for the intended send path.

### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

Every inbound iMessage in a direct conversation includes a `reply_to_id` field pointing at the immediately preceding message — even when the user did not use iMessage's native reply/swipe gesture and simply typed and sent a normal message. This makes `reply_to_id` indistinguishable from "previous message in the conversation," rather than reflecting a genuine user-initiated reply relationship.

A related effect: because the agent's own internal reasoning/tool-use narration is sometimes delivered as a separate message from its actual final answer, the "reply target" resolved for the user's next message can end up being that internal-dialog message — not the message that actually contains the content the user is responding to. The two are sometimes bundled together and sometimes not, so the reply target is inconsistent even from the same conversation flow, reproduces on 2026.7.1-2 and 2026.9.4.

### Steps to reproduce

1. In an active iMessage DM with the agent, send a normal message (no swipe-to-reply, no tapback-reply — just type and hit send)
2. Inspect the internal context passed to the model
3. Observe `reply_to_id` is populated, pointing at the prior message, along with a fully resolved "Reply target of current user message" block
4. Note that the resolved reply target is often a long internal-narration message (agent reasoning/tool commentary) rather than the specific content the user meant to respond to

### Expected behavior

`reply_to_id` should only be populated when the user actually performs a native reply action (e.g., swipe-to-reply in Messages.app), and should be absent/null for ordinary sequential messages. When it is populated, it should point at a coherent, user-facing message — not an arbitrary internal-narration fragment that happened to be the most recent bubble.

### Actual behavior

`reply_to_id` is populated on effectively every message regardless of any reply gesture, and resolves to whatever the most recent message happens to be — including agent internal-dialog/narration content that isn't the actual reply target the user intended.

### OpenClaw version

2026.9.4

### Operating system

macOS 15.7

### Install method

npm global

### Model

anthropic/claud-sonnet-5

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw -> opencode zen -> anthropic

### Additional provider/model setup details

iMessage channel connected to agent dedicated apple id conversing with another apple id.

### Logs

```shell

```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Example payload from a message that was just typed normally, not replied to anything:

{"chat_id":"chat_id:2","message_id":"2137","reply_to_id":"4D503960-ADED-410C-A9D8-5D34E4DF2C50","was_mentioned":true}
A later example in the same conversation resolved `reply_to_id` to an entire prior multi-paragraph agent message (reasoning + a full draft bug report embedded in it) — again with no reply gesture performed by the user.


### Impact and severity

Affected: iMessage channels from 2026.7.1-2 and 2026.9.4; signal channel on same installs seems to not be affected.
Severity: Low-to-moderate- any consumer relying on `reply_to_id` to detect genuine reply intent (vs. plain sequential chat) will get false positives on every message, and the resolved "reply target" content can be misleading (internal narration rather than the intended answer).

### Additional information

Seems to be new behavior since upgrading in 2026.7.x; remains in 2026.9.x

 Channel: iMessage (direct message)
• Reproduced across 2 independent sessions, multiple consecutive normal (non-reply) messages, consistent every time

### Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.9.5 (ec9c1a1), Gateway as a systemd service on Linux x64 (Debian-based NAS), Node v24.21.0
- Automation job: cron `0 11 * * 1-5` (Asia/Shanghai), payload `agentTurn` (`timeoutSeconds: 3600`), `sessionTarget: "current"`, `delivery: announce` to the owning Telegram direct-chat session
- Agent model `zai/glm-5.3` via openai-completions; the scheduled turn is a long analysis run (~8–9 min, ~1M total tokens incl. cache reads)

### What happened

Two consecutive weekday runs of the same job failed at the agent-run layer with:

```
attempt disposed before transcript write
```

- Run 1 — started 2026-09-22T03:00:00Z, duration 486s → `completionStatus: failed`, error `attempt disposed before transcript write` (diagnostics source: `agent-run`), delivery status `unknown`. Usage recorded: 98,240 input / 20,353 output tokens.
- Run 2 — started 2026-09-23T03:00:00Z, duration 249s → same error. Usage recorded: 96,954 input / 10,403 output tokens.

Notable details:

- Both runs **did consume full model output** (10k–20k output tokens) before dying, so the attempt was disposed at persist time, not at request time.
- The Gateway process stayed up through both windows — the lifecycle restart log shows no stop/restart, and memory was healthy (14 GB total, ~10 GB available). So this is not a restart kill or OOM.
- Intermittent: the same job succeeded on 2026-09-21 (560s, delivered normally) and on 2026-09-24 the analysis itself completed (529s — its delivery failed separately, see companion issue). 2 of the last 4 scheduled runs failed this way.

### Impact

The entire scheduled run's work is lost for the day — no summary is persisted anywhere retrievable, and the analysis had to be re-run manually. The job only reports `attempt disposed before transcript write` with no further stack trace in the run diagnostics.

### Related

- #143581 — same error string on the inbound chat surface (spool retry loop)
- #143580 — heartbeat-lane continuation sent without transcript
- #113019 — closed; session write-lock orphaned after an aborted turn
- #141132 — closed; per-attempt AsyncLocalStorage never disabled, degrading awaits

Our surface (scheduled `agentTurn` automation runs) appears distinct from the reports above, so filing separately — happy to merge if maintainers see one root cause.

Companion issue for the delivery-side race on the same job (`session rebound` during announce delivery): #156983

issues.body:
### Summary

Add a **bounded launch contract** for Swarm `agents.run` so a verification lane can be stricter than an ordinary collector without gaining new authority.

Implementation: #155442.

### Proposed API

`agents.run(..., { boundedLaunch })` may specify:

- `boundary: "isolated" | "summary-only" | "evidence-only" | "artifact-only"`;
- `requirements.sandbox: "require"`;
- required candidate/artifact fields;
- a `candidateBinding` containing candidate/source/recipe/policy digests.

The contract is monotone: it can only remove explicit handoff information or request stricter existing admission. It cannot grant tools, credentials, approval, publish, merge, or deploy authority.

### Architecture boundary

This is the freeze/seal measurement seam:

`explore -> select -> freeze/seal exact candidate -> bounded launch -> verify`

That vocabulary matches current OpenClaw concepts: frozen/sealed candidates, candidate bindings, and bounded launch contracts.

Adaptive population dynamics, novelty/disagreement/correlation feedback, phase classification, sampling temperature, and compute allocation remain caller/plugin policy (#158068), not core launch authority.

### Ownership

- `sessions_spawn` owns admission/execution.
- The existing sandbox path owns sandbox admission.
- The registry owns replay/idempotency.
- Existing tool/source policy remains authoritative.

### Evidence

#155442 proves boundary projection, authority-shaped-field rejection, fail-closed sandbox admission, exact candidate binding, replay invalidation across candidate/source/recipe/policy, legacy behavior, and real native-path execution.

### Product decision requested

Should OpenClaw expose this narrow generic bounded-launch primitive in core?

Maintainer edits are enabled.

issues.body:
## Summary

Prompt-cache invalidation caused by unstable system-prompt content is a **recurring bug class**, not a series of isolated incidents. It has been fixed and has regressed at least twice, and there are currently several open instances at once.

This asks for a **structural guarantee** that the cached prefix is byte-stable across turns, rather than another point fix that the next volatile field will defeat.

## Evidence that this is a class

| issue | state | instance |
|---|---|---|
| [#19989](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/19989) | closed | prompt cache constantly invalidated, ~10x cost |
| [#18963](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/18963) | closed | cache misses on most turns in auto-reply path |
| [#3658](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/3658) | closed | injected timestamps for TUI/web messages |
| [#140129](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/140129) | open | cache stuck at ~46k on long sessions |
| [#146902](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/146902) | open | same-session tool-set churn |
| [#155685](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/155685) | closed | rewind mints a new `sessionId` **inside the cached region** |
| [#155742](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/155742) | open | two tool schemas alternate between capability profiles |
| [#155868](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/155868) | open | agent-sourced runs get a reduced tool roster |
| [#143017](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/143017) | open | Prompt-cache: five ways a persistent session rewrites its prefix |
| [#150081](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/150081) | open | Possible prompt-cache regression on sessions_yield/announce |
| [#128014](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/128014) | open | Prompt-cache invalidation in long Anthropic sessions |

Four closed, seven open. Every one is the same underlying failure: **something above the cache breakpoint changed when it did not need to.**

## Root observation

The architecture already intends stability. The system prompt is split by `splitSystemPromptCacheBoundary()` into a stable prefix and a dynamic suffix, marked in the text with `<!-- openclaw:attempt:STABLE -->` and `<!-- openclaw:attempt:DYNAMIC -->`, and the cache trace digests them separately:

```js
systemPromptDigest: digestText(splitSystemPrompt?.stablePrefix ?? params.systemPrompt),
...splitSystemPrompt ? { systemPromptSuffixDigest: digestText(splitSystemPrompt.dynamicSuffix) } : {},
```

The problem is that the block named `DYNAMIC` is **still inside the cached region**. In one local sample, 12 of 18 observed cache-break events listed the system prompt suffix among their changes. So the "dynamic" section is not free — anything volatile placed there invalidates the whole conversation cache.

That is how #155685 happens: a `sessionId` is interpolated into a `Runtime:` line in that block. The split exists; **nothing enforces that volatile content ends up on the cheap side of it.**

## Measured cost

From one local session (OpenClaw 2026.9.5, `claude-opus-5`, `cacheRetention: long`):

```
16:28  human turn                       read=107112  write=1268     warm
16:38  4-character inter-agent message  read=0       write=159387   total miss
17:23  ordinary human turn              read=41970   write=137866   partial miss
17:27  ordinary human turn              read=185925  write=1013     warm
```

A four-character message payload cost **159,387 cache-write tokens**. Four of eleven consecutive turns missed or read at a floor.

---

## Proposal A — persist the system prompt per session

1. **Store the rendered system prompt with the session** rather than regenerating it every turn. Reuse the stored string verbatim on subsequent turns.
2. **Regenerate only at moments when the cache is already gone**, namely when any of the following holds:
   - **(a)** more than `cacheRetention` has elapsed since the last turn, so the provider-side entry has expired anyway;
   - **(b)** the user explicitly asks, via a command such as `/refresh_system_prompt`;
   - **(c)** **compaction has occurred**, since compaction rewrites the head of message history and the conversation cache is already lost at that point;
   - **(d)** a correctness-critical fact changed — see the constraints section below.
3. **Record the user-message count at generation time** in the stored prompt, so the model can tell how far the conversation has moved since it was rendered.

The unifying principle behind point 2 is worth stating explicitly, because it is what makes the whole proposal cheap:

> **Regeneration should only ever happen at a moment when the cache is already cold, or must be discarded for correctness. Then a refresh never costs anything that was not already lost.**

That principle generalises beyond this feature: any unavoidable prompt change should be deferred to the next already-cold turn where correctness permits.

### Staleness disclosure (point 3)

The count is **captured at generation time and frozen into the stored prompt**, not re-evaluated per turn. It therefore changes only when the prompt is regenerated, which by point 2 only happens when the cache is already cold. It is cache-safe.

The general rule it must satisfy — and does — is that **anything added to the system prompt in order to describe volatility must not itself be volatile.** A counter re-evaluated every turn would be self-defeating, converting an occasional miss into a permanent one.

**Interaction with compaction, and why trigger (c) matters.** Without (c), this mechanism would quietly break. Compaction replaces earlier user turns with a single `compactionSummary`, so the number of user messages *visible* to the model drops below the frozen count. The model would then infer that the prompt is *fresher* than it is — a silent failure biased toward "not stale", which is the wrong direction for a staleness signal. Regenerating on compaction re-bases the count at exactly the moment history is rewritten, so the comparison stays valid.

**Lower-risk variant.** The mechanism still asks the model to count its own user messages, which is unreliable over a long transcript. Since the gateway knows both numbers, it can do the arithmetic instead:

- system prompt (frozen, cached): `System context generated at session message #<N>.`
- per-turn user-role context (appended, outside the cached region): `System context is <K> messages and <T> minutes old.`

This is exact, needs no model arithmetic, and the varying half lives in the appended user-role block that already carries sender identity and conversation metadata (`buildInboundUserContextPrefix()`), so it costs nothing in cache terms.

Either way, a bare number is inert unless it says what to do about it. Worth naming the fields that can actually go stale:

> System context may be stale. Verify date, model identity and tool availability with `session_status` rather than relying on this block.

### Correctness constraints on freezing

Some content must force regeneration under (d), because a stale value is a correctness bug rather than a cosmetic one:

- **Tool roster.** Tools are transmitted separately from the system prompt. A frozen `## Tooling` section that lists tools no longer present, or omits newly added ones, actively misleads the model. (See #155868 and #146902 — the roster is currently varying for reasons unrelated to config.)
- **Model identity**, when a session switches models mid-conversation.
- **Elevated access and exec approval state**, where a stale value has security consequences.
- **Date**, for sessions spanning midnight — although this is a good candidate for deferral under the point-2 rule rather than an immediate regeneration.

---

## Proposal B — volatility-typed prompt sections (complementary)

Proposal A fixes the current instances. This one makes the class structurally impossible.

Have each prompt section declare its volatility at assembly time:

```ts
type PromptSectionVolatility = "stable" | "per-session" | "per-turn";
```

The assembler then places `per-turn` content **after the last cache breakpoint** automatically, and a test asserts that no `per-turn` section can be emitted above it.

This removes reliance on authors remembering which side of an invisible boundary their new field lands on — which is the actual historical failure mode. Every issue in the table above is someone adding a reasonable field without knowing it was cache-relevant. The marker comments are easy to miss, and the field name `systemPromptDigest` actively suggests the whole prompt is covered when it is only the stable prefix.

## Proposal C — move per-turn content out of the system prompt entirely

Narrower and cheapest to implement. The `Message Context` block and the `Runtime:` line carry per-turn and per-session values (`sessionId`, channel, surface, chat type) inside the cached region. Sender identity is **already** handled correctly by being placed in the user-role prefix instead.

Extending that existing treatment to the remaining per-turn fields would resolve #155685 directly and shrink the surface for recurrences, without introducing persistence.

## Proposal D — regression guard

Whichever of the above is adopted, a regression test would prevent a third round of this:

> Run N turns in one session with no configuration change, and assert the cached prefix digest is byte-identical across all of them.

Given that #19989 and #18963 were both closed and the class returned, a guard test is arguably the highest-value single item in this request.

---

## Observability asks

These made the current investigation much harder than it needed to be:

1. **`systemPromptDigest` covers only the stable prefix**, not the whole system prompt. This is easy to misread; an entire day of local diagnosis was spent measuring the wrong field and drawing a false negative from it. Consider renaming to `systemPromptStablePrefixDigest`.
2. **`broke` is unreliable.** A `cacheRead == 0` total miss was reported `broke: false`, while a partial read on the following request was reported `broke: true`.
3. **No provenance in the snapshot.** `cache:state` records `toolDigest`, `toolCount` and `toolNames`, but nothing about *why* a given roster or prompt variant was selected. Classifying runs required joining against the `prompt:before` stage.

---

*Filed from local diagnostics on 2026.9.5 plus source reading. Happy to supply the analysis scripts, the raw measurements, or to test a proposed patch.*

## Summary

Subagent runs spawned from a cron "dispatcher" session can stay `running` in the subagent registry forever, even though the child session is recorded as `done` in the session store. The explicit `timeoutSeconds` on the spawn never fires, the registry sweeper's session-store fallback does not reconcile them, and they survive gateway restarts. Each one also holds a `pending` completion delivery and a `running` TaskFlow, so `openclaw tasks audit` reports them as `stale_running` while `openclaw tasks maintenance` proposes 0 reconcile / 0 recovered.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.9.4 (3a9d69d), macOS 15.6 arm64, Node 26.5.0
- Child subagent model provider: openai via codex-app-server mirror (`mirrorOrigin: codex-app-server` on the transcript entries)
- Spawn shape (from a cron `agentTurn` payload): `sessions_spawn` with `runtime: subagent`, `mode: run`, `context: isolated`, `lightContext: true`, `timeoutSeconds: 3600`, `cleanup: keep`; the cron run then ends immediately without `sessions_yield` and with cron `delivery.mode = none`.

## Observed

`openclaw tasks list --status running --json` shows 11 subagent tasks, ages 25h to 199h, all `deliveryStatus: pending`, `progressSummary: null`. Example:

```
taskId a8a8a200-… runtime=subagent status=running deliveryStatus=pending
startedAt 2026-09-21T10:25:14Z lastEventAt 2026-09-21T10:39:24Z toolUseCount=36 lastToolName=exec
childSessionKey agent:<agent>:subagent:ac51f983-…  runId 1e959bc3-…
```

The child session in the agent sqlite store (`session_nodes.entry_json`) for that key:

```
status = "done"   startedAt 10:27Z   endedAt 10:41Z   abortedLastRun = false   runtimeMs = 833632
lastRunId = "image_generate:447f744c-…:ok:agent-loop"
activeWriterRunId = "image_generate:447f744c-…:ok:agent-loop"
```

`session_windows` for the same key: `status=done, started 10:27:52, ended 10:41:45`.

So the child finished normally two minutes after the registry's last event, but the terminal turn was attributed to an `image_generate:…:agent-loop` run id rather than the subagent's own run id (`1e959bc3-…`). The registry never observed a completion for `1e959bc3-…`.

Gateway log around that time has only:

```
diagnostic: lane wait exceeded: lane=session:agent:<agent>:subagent:ac51f983-… waitedMs=692248 queueAhead=0 activeAhead=1 activeNow=0
```

Nothing afterwards for that run: no timeout, no completion, no announce attempt.

Registry sweeper keeps logging (every minute) `subagent suspended delivery backlog exceeded pressure cap` with `suspendedCount` 46–48 against `hardCap: 50`; separate issue, but the stuck runs add to the same admission pressure.

## Expected

One of:
1. The registry should treat the child session's persisted terminal state (`status: done`, `endedAt` set, `abortedLastRun: false`, `endedAt >= entry.startedAt`) as completion of the subagent run during the sweep, regardless of which run id wrote the final turn.
2. `timeoutSeconds` on the spawn should be enforced by the registry independently of the live agent-run context, so a wedged context still ends after the explicit limit.
3. `openclaw tasks maintenance --apply` (or restart recovery, `reconcileOrphanedRestoredRuns` with `includeStaleUnended`) should reconcile `stale_running` entries older than `STALE_UNENDED_SUBAGENT_RUN_MS` when the session store shows the session ended.

Right now the only remedy is a manual `openclaw tasks cancel <taskId>` per run.

## Reading dist

- `subagent-registry-*.mjs` `sweepOnce()`: unended entries only reach `resolveCompletionFromSessionEntry()` when `!getAgentRunContext(runId)`; if a context lingers the entry is treated as live indefinitely.
- `subagent-completion-admission.store-*.mjs` `resolveSubagentRunOrphanReason()` only returns `stale-unended` when `includeStaleUnended` is set, which happens on restore only, and restore skips entries with `execution.restartRecovery` set.

Happy to provide the sanitised registry dump for the 11 entries.

issues.body:
## Summary

The tooling TypeScript loader (`scripts/tsx.mjs` → `registerToolingTsx()`) pins `TSX_TSCONFIG_PATH` only when the caller cwd lacks a tsconfig **and** the shim's own checkout root has one. Derived checkouts — copied `scripts/` trees used by fixtures and wrappers — have no `tsconfig.json` at their root, so the pin silently declines and workspace imports fail with a deep `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. Make the loader resolve its source checkout through the configured pnpm modules dir as a fallback, and fail fast with an actionable message when no tsconfig can be found anywhere.

## Problem to solve

- The `@openclaw/*` workspace packages used by `src/` (e.g. `@openclaw/normalization-core`) are not declared in the root `package.json` and are not linked into root `node_modules` (verified in this checkout; only `tsconfig` `paths` map them). That makes tsx's tsconfig discovery load-bearing for any source-graph import.
- tsx discovers the tsconfig from the caller cwd. From a cwd without one, paths mapping is off, and failures surface as `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` deep inside the import graph with no hint about cwd/tsconfig/loader state.
- #152875 adds a pin for the common case (explicit env unset **and** cwd has no tsconfig **and** the shim checkout has one). That condition deliberately declines for derived checkouts whose root lacks `tsconfig.json`, so every caller must rediscover the workaround: `test/scripts/run-node-lifecycle.test.ts` now hand-sets `TSX_TSCONFIG_PATH` in two fixture env builders alongside `PNPM_CONFIG_MODULES_DIR`.
- There is no fail-fast diagnostic: "pin declined because no tsconfig exists anywhere" is indistinguishable from a genuinely missing package until the deep resolver error appears.
- The product surface was solved at a different layer: generated agent-cli shims export `TSX_TSCONFIG_PATH` via `resolveCurrentOpenClawCliInvocation` (`src/infra/openclaw-cli-invocation.ts`), per the fix lineage of #131322. The tooling loader has no equivalent fallback for derived checkouts.

## Proposed solution

1. Keep the precedence explicit: explicit `TSX_TSCONFIG_PATH` > cwd tsconfig > shim-checkout tsconfig (the pin introduced in #152875).
2. Add a fallback: when the shim checkout has no tsconfig, derive the source checkout from the configured pnpm modules dir (`PNPM_CONFIG_MODULES_DIR` / `npm_config_modules_dir` — the same provenance fixture callers already pass so the shim can find `tsx`) and pin that checkout's `tsconfig.json`.
3. If no candidate resolves, fail fast in `registerToolingTsx()` with an error that names `TSX_TSCONFIG_PATH` and the expected checkout tsconfig, instead of a deep module-not-found.
4. Document the contract next to the documented loader invocation (`.agents/skills/openclaw-live-updater/SKILL.md`, `docs/reference/test/runner-internals.md`), and remove the now-redundant fixture env pins in the same PR, with tests proving the loader owns it.

## Alternatives considered

- **Declare the `@openclaw/*` workspace packages in the root `package.json`** (suggested in #131322): they are private, unpublished workspace packages, so they cannot be dependencies of the published package, and native entry without a loader still fails on `.js`→`.ts` specifiers — loader + paths mapping remains required for source-mode flows.
- **Stage a `tsconfig.json` into every fixture checkout**: multiplies fixture boilerplate and drifts from real checkouts.
- **Force `cwd` to the checkout root in every spawn**: contradicts fixtures and agent exec that must run from arbitrary cwd by design (the expected behavior in #131322).

## Impact

- **Affected:** repo test fixtures (`run-node-lifecycle`, `openclaw-live-updater`), CI lanes spawning checkout tooling from temp cwds, any future derived copy of `scripts/`.
- **Severity:** Medium — hard, cryptic failures; scattered per-caller workarounds drift over time.
- **Frequency:** Every derived-checkout or foreign-cwd spawn without an explicit env pin.
- **Consequence:** red suites exactly of the shape #152875 had to repair; each new caller re-discovers `TSX_TSCONFIG_PATH`; the silent-failure class reported in #131322 (empty stdout read as empty data).

## Evidence/examples

Reproduced on Node 24.16.0 (copied `scripts/` tree into a temp checkout without `tsconfig.json`; cwd a fresh temp directory):

- **A — copied checkout, no env:** `TSX_TSCONFIG_PATH = undefined` → `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND: Cannot find package '@openclaw/normalization-core' imported from src/cli/profile.ts`
- **B — same with `TSX_TSCONFIG_PATH=<checkout>/tsconfig.json`:** resolves (`applyCliProfileEnv, parseCliProfileArgs`)
- **C — real checkout shim, same foreign cwd:** pin applies → `TSX_TSCONFIG_PATH = <checkout>/tsconfig.json` → resolves

Related history: #152875 (loader pin for the common foreign-cwd case), #131322 (prior product-surface report), and the fixture env pins in `test/scripts/run-node-lifecycle.test.ts`.

## Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this myself

## Additional information

The fix extends the pin introduced in #152875, so its PR will follow or stack on that change. This issue is filed first per CONTRIBUTING: "For agent-authored or otherwise non-trivial work, create or reuse the issue first, then open the PR against it."

issues.body:
### Summary

Allow custom Control UI sidebar groups to contain subgroups, creating a hierarchy for organizing sessions and projects.

### Problem to solve

Sidebar groups are currently flat. Once users maintain many long-running sessions across several areas, the list becomes long and hard to scan. For example, top-level areas such as Work and Personal cannot contain project groups such as SAP, Finance, Family, or School. Prefixes and emoji only imitate hierarchy; they do not provide structural grouping or independent collapse state.

### Proposed solution

Support hierarchical custom sidebar groups.

Suggested behavior:
- A group can optionally have a parent group (at least two levels; arbitrary depth would be even better).
- Sessions can be assigned to any group in the tree.
- Parent and child groups are independently collapsible, with collapse state persisted.
- The UI can create, move, rename, reorder, and delete nested groups, including sensible handling of children when a parent is removed.
- Existing session/group tools and APIs expose the hierarchy.
- Existing flat groups remain valid root groups with no migration work required.

### Alternatives considered

Name prefixes such as `WORK / SAP` or emoji section headers help visually, but they remain one flat list and cannot be collapsed as a unit. Separate agents or workspaces provide isolation, but are too heavyweight when the need is only navigation and organization.

### Impact

Affected: Users with many concurrent or long-running sessions/projects.
Severity: Persistent UX friction; it does not block work, but makes navigation increasingly cumbersome.
Frequency: Constant once the sidebar contains more than a handful of groups.
Consequence: More scrolling, slower session switching, and manual naming conventions to simulate hierarchy.

### Evidence/examples

A representative sidebar may already have root groups such as OpenClaw, SAP, Local First Stack, Blog+Social, Finance, Health, Family, and School. Several naturally belong under broader folders such as Work or Personal, but the current flat model cannot express that.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

No, proposing the idea only

### Additional information

Please preserve backward compatibility: existing groups should behave exactly as root-level groups. A stable parent reference would avoid coupling hierarchy to display-name separators, but the implementation is flexible.

### Bug type

Native iOS release/distribution bug

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

The native Skill Workshop fix for revision-bound proposal actions exists in current repository source, but it is not in the iOS binary currently distributed through the Apple App Store.

OpenClaw's iOS release owner needs to submit and release a fixed build (2026.8.11 or later) through App Store Connect. Apple can then review and distribute that submitted build; Apple is not the owner of the code fix or release submission.

### Why this is a new issue

#137051 was closed after the bot validated the **web Control UI** in v2026.8.2. The reported failure came from the **native iOS app**, and the reporter cannot reopen the maintainer-closed issue (`viewerCanReopen: false`). This issue tracks the remaining native mobile release action only.

### Current released behavior

Apple's German App Store currently serves OpenClaw iOS version 2026.8.10. In its matching release ref, the native Swift Skill Workshop sends `IPadSkillProposalInspectParams` for `skills.proposals.apply` / `skills.proposals.reject`, so the request contains `agentId` and `proposalId` but omits the Gateway-required `expectedRevisionHash`.

The Gateway therefore rejects Apply with:

```text
skills.proposals.apply: [INVALID_REQUEST]
invalid skills.proposals.apply params: must have required property 'expectedRevisionHash'
```

The proposal remains pending.

### Source and release evidence

- Public App Store version: 2026.8.10: https://apps.apple.com/de/app/openclaw-ai-that-does-things/id6780396132
- iOS 2026.8.10 release ref: `refs/openclaw/mobile-releases/ios/2026.8.10-1` at `dd66075f0123010a7d171934124c80ae920badda` (cut Aug 9).
- Faulty native request builder: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/dd66075f0123010a7d171934124c80ae920badda/apps/ios/Sources/Design/IPadSkillWorkshopScreen.swift#L871-L885
- Revision-binding fix: `94eb34fa78088f1a8fe33bbe2736279273997d77` (Aug 19), after the 2026.8.10 mobile cut: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/94eb34fa78088f1a8fe33bbe2736279273997d77
- iOS 2026.8.11 release ref: `refs/openclaw/mobile-releases/ios/2026.8.11-1` at `93706992214eae5785e8dbf9ea9020a3c2bd7511`, containing the corrected native request: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/93706992214eae5785e8dbf9ea9020a3c2bd7511/apps/ios/Sources/Design/IPadSkillWorkshopScreen.swift#L1134-L1153
- Native regression test verifies JSON contains `expectedRevisionHash`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/93706992214eae5785e8dbf9ea9020a3c2bd7511/apps/ios/Tests/RootTabsPresentationTests.swift#L411-L428

### Reproduction validation

A separate v2026.8.2 Gateway environment reproduced the exact `INVALID_REQUEST` with the 2026.8.10 native request shape. The same request with the proposal's inspected `expectedRevisionHash` succeeded. No production proposal was changed.

### Expected behavior

The publicly distributed native iOS app includes the existing revision-bound action code and sends `expectedRevisionHash` for Skill Workshop apply/reject operations.

### Actual behavior

The public iOS 2026.8.10 binary predates that fix and cannot apply valid proposals from the native Skill Workshop screen.

### Versions

- Public native iOS app: 2026.8.10
- Gateway used for reproduction: 2026.8.2 (`0965053`)
- Fixed native source: iOS 2026.8.11 release ref or later

### Requested resolution

The OpenClaw iOS release owner should submit and release the already-fixed native iOS build through App Store Connect. Close this issue only after the fixed binary is publicly downloadable and the native Apply flow is smoke-tested against a current Gateway.

issues.body:
# Gateway: runaway RSS outside V8 heap causes host OOM and shutdown timeout

## Environment

- OpenClaw `2026.9.5`
- Node.js `26.4.0`
- Linux x64
- Gateway as a systemd user service
- Host memory visible to the service: ~15 GiB

## Incident

On 2026-09-20, the Gateway reached `9.32 GiB` RSS with only `962 MiB` V8 heap used. The Linux OOM killer terminated processes in `openclaw-gateway.service` repeatedly between 18:48 and 19:04; the Gateway was eventually killed and restarted.

The issue is reproducible after a fresh restart: RSS grows to roughly `2–4 GiB` within minutes, while V8 heap remains around `620–700 MiB`.

## Evidence

- Stability sample: RSS `2.12 GiB`, heap used `638 MiB`.
- Shortly after: RSS `3.50 GiB`, heap used `620 MiB`.
- Heap profile capture: heap used fell from `722 MiB` to `673 MiB`, while RSS rose from `2.48 GiB` to `2.73 GiB` during the 5-second sample.
- V8 external memory was only ~30 MiB and ArrayBuffers ~6 MiB.
- A persisted stability bundle before shutdown recorded RSS `4.75 GiB` with heap used `1.41 GiB`.
- The heap profile did not identify a large JavaScript allocation owner. SQLite-related sample allocations were small.
- Startup also logged `MaxListenersExceededWarning: Possible EventEmitter memory leak detected. 11 exit listeners added to [process].`

This points to native allocation/retention, allocator fragmentation, or a loaded integration outside normal V8 heap accounting.

## Operational impact

The Gateway service previously used `TimeoutStopSec=330`. During controlled restart it exceeded the graceful shutdown window, producing `gateway.stop_shutdown_timeout` and extending downtime.

## Temporary mitigations applied

- 4 GiB swap added to avoid host-wide OOM.
- systemd service guard: `MemoryHigh=5G`, `MemoryMax=6G`.
- `TimeoutStopSec=60s`.
- Runtime options: `--max-old-space-size=4096 --trace-warnings` and `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2`.

These protect the host and improve recovery but do not resolve the RSS growth.

## Request

Please advise on collecting attribution for non-V8 RSS and on known regressions in `2026.9.5` involving Gateway native memory growth, spawn-broker/service-child supervision, MCP/plugin loading, or shutdown listener accumulation.

A payload-free diagnostics archive was generated locally with `openclaw gateway diagnostics export` and can be shared through an appropriate private channel if needed.

issues.body:
### Environment

- openclaw 2026.8.2 (regression vs 2026.7.1-2), gateway on Linux
- Channel: community `@openclaw/feishu` plugin (CardKit streaming card)
- Dashboard / control-ui shows live progress the whole time (separate event path)

### Behavior

After upgrading 2026.7.1-2 → 2026.8.2, channels that implement neither `onBlockReply` (block streaming) nor the new `streaming.mode: "progress"` rendering receive **no partial updates during tool-execution phases**. On Feishu the streaming card stays frozen while the agent works (tool calls and inter-tool assistant text are all visible on the dashboard), then the final answer arrives as one big dump at the end.

### Root cause

In the embedded-agent subscribe layer (`dist/builtin-openclaw-*.js`), `handleMessageUpdate` / `handleMessageEnd` now early-return for assistant messages with `phase === "commentary"`, emitting only to the dashboard path without the `emitPartialReply` option:

```js
// commentary branch → dashboard only
ctx.emitAssistantStreamData(commentaryData); // no { emitPartialReply: true }
```

The channel delivery gate requires `delivery.emitPartialReply && params.onPartialReply && state.shouldEmitPartialReplies`, so `onPartialReply` never fires for commentary text. In 2026.7.1-2 these texts carried no commentary marker and reached channels via `ctx.emitAssistantStreamData(data, { emitPartialReply: true })`.

For channels that never provide an `onBlockReply` callback (the feishu plugin doesn't, so `streaming.block.enabled` is a no-op for it) and that have no progress-mode rendering (the feishu plugin implements no progress compositor), **there is no remaining path to receive inter-tool text at all** — hence the regression.

### Suggested fix

Any of:

1. When the active channel provides neither `onBlockReply` nor progress-mode rendering, fall back to delivering commentary partials with `emitPartialReply: true`;
2. Implement a progress-mode fallback in channels that only support plain partial streaming;
3. At minimum, document that commentary streaming requires a progress-capable channel.

### Local workaround (verified)

Added `{ emitPartialReply: true }` at the commentary emit sites in `handleMessageUpdate` (commentary branch) and `emitAssistantCommentaryStreamData`. After the patch the Feishu card streams inter-tool text again; dashboard unaffected.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect state / command failure)

### Summary

On Windows, `openclaw gateway install --force` consistently fails while publishing the Scheduled Task launcher:

```text
Gateway install failed: AggregateError: Task launcher changed during publication: C:\Users\<user>\.openclaw\gateway.cmd
The previous service definition could not be restored.
The previous service definition could not be restored.
```

The failure is stable across retries and occurs after the new `gateway.cmd` has been written. `@openclaw/fs-safe`'s `replaceFileAtomic` refreshes the target file's `mtimeMs` by roughly 10 ms during publication, while `matchesServiceFilePublication` in `src/daemon/service-stage.ts` requires `mtimeMs` to exactly equal the staged temp file's value.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Windows 10/11, Node v24.20.0, OpenClaw 2026.10.5 installed via npm global.
2. An existing Windows Scheduled Task named `OpenClaw Gateway` (enabled, disabled, or running).
3. Run `openclaw gateway install --force`.
4. Observe the error above; `gateway.cmd.bak` and `gateway.cmd.task.xml.bak` are left beside the launcher, and the task definition is not updated.

### Evidence

A minimal reproduction using the same `publishServiceFile` path against a copy of `gateway.cmd` in a temp directory produced:

```text
prepared {"sha256":"6ebd374312ef...","mode":438,"dev":2316905573,"ino":16325548649589748,"size":594,"mtimeMs":1792378718915.6643,"ctimeMs":1792378718917.667}
current  {"sha256":"6ebd374312ef...","mode":438,"dev":2316905573,"ino":16325548649589748,"size":594,"mtimeMs":1792378718925.69,"ctimeMs":1792378718925.69}
DIFF mtimeMs 1792378718915.6643 -> 1792378718925.69
```

Only `mtimeMs` differs. `sha256`, `size`, `ino`, `dev`, and `mode` are identical. A standalone `fs.rename` test in the same directory preserves `mtimeMs`, so the refresh appears to come from the fs-safe publication path rather than NTFS rename semantics. `chkdsk C: /scan` reports no problems.

### Relevant source

`src/daemon/service-stage.ts`:

```ts
return (
  current !== null &&
  (["dev", "ino"] as const).every(...) &&
  (["sha256", "mode", "size", "mtimeMs"] as const).every(
    (key) => current[key] === prepared[key],
  )
);
```

`matchesServiceFilePublication` is also used by the macOS LaunchAgent publication path, but the observed failure is on Windows.

### Expected behavior

`gateway install --force` should either:

- compare only stable publication facts (`dev`, `ino`, `sha256`, `mode`, `size`), or
- compare the post-rename `mtime` instead of the staged temp file's `mtime`.

As a local workaround, removing `"mtimeMs"` from the compared fields makes `openclaw gateway install --force` complete and rebuilds the Scheduled Task correctly (S4U, BootTrigger + LogonTrigger, `cmd.exe /d /s /c "<script>"`, WorkingDirectory set).

### Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.10.5 (1b58cb9), npm global install
- Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 (10.0.19044)
- Node v24.20.0
- State directory: ~87k files / ~3 GB (relevant to startup latency, not to this check)
- Gateway auth uses a SecretRef-managed token (`source: store`); the install warning about not persisting the resolved token is present but unrelated.

issues.body:
### Summary

Let operators pick the uid/gid the Compose services run as, so OpenClaw works on hosts whose bind-mount directories are not owned by uid 1000.

### Problem to solve

Docker bind mounts carry ownership numerically: the container sees the host's uid/gid, never its user names. A write succeeds only when the container's uid owns the mounted directory, or reaches it through its gid.

The runtime image runs as `USER node` (uid 1000) and there is no supported way to change that. Every host whose data directories belong to a different uid therefore fails at first write with `EACCES` on `/home/node/.openclaw`:

- a Linux account that happens to be uid 1001 or higher
- CI runners and build agents
- LDAP- or NFS-mapped home directories
- network-attached storage and NAS appliances, where the owning uid is assigned by the platform

Today `docs/install/docker/compose-operations.md` answers this with `sudo chown -R 1000:1000 <dirs>`. That works when you own the directories, and is impossible when you do not — shared storage, an owner you do not control, or a uid policy you cannot change. There is no second branch.

Related but distinct, for context: #34594 (idmap for `docker.binds`/`workspaceAccess`) and #126631 both concern the agent sandbox's mounts, not the Gateway container's own identity.

### Proposed solution

Set the runtime identity at the Compose layer rather than in the image, so no root process is ever involved:

```yaml
user: "${OPENCLAW_PUID:-1000}:${OPENCLAW_PGID:-1000}"
```

on both `openclaw-gateway` and `openclaw-cli`. Unset resolves to `1000:1000`, which is exactly the image's `node` user, so existing deployments are byte-for-byte unchanged and the `Dockerfile` needs no edit at all.

Two supporting pieces are required for a non-1000 uid to actually work:

1. `/home/node` stays uid-1000-owned, so `HOME`-derived caches must be redirected into the writable state mount (`XDG_CACHE_HOME`, `NPM_CONFIG_CACHE`). This is the same redirection `src/fleet/cell-profile.ts` and `scripts/podman/openclaw.container.in` already perform, and `scripts/e2e/fleet-cache-docker.sh` already asserts the pairing (`cacheOwnerUid === process.getuid()` together with `imageHomeOwnerUid === 1000`).
2. `scripts/docker/setup.sh` should validate the values and target its existing brief-root ownership repair at the configured owner instead of the hardcoded `node:node`.

The Gateway should also refuse to start when an explicitly requested identity still resolves to uid 0, keyed off the request rather than "am I root" — fleet cells deliberately run `--user 0:0` on a rootless daemon and must keep working.

### Alternatives considered

- **Root entrypoint with `usermod`/`setpriv` (the LinuxServer.io PUID/PGID pattern).** Rejected: it breaks the verbatim-pinned `ENTRYPOINT`/`CMD` in `src/dockerfile.test.ts`, leaves a root PID 1 and root `docker compose exec` shells, breaks fleet cells on rootless Docker (which run the image with no entrypoint override), and its per-start unattended chown launders plugin-directory ownership past the `src/plugins/discovery.ts` gate.
- **Making the image arbitrary-uid friendly** (`chmod 1777 /home/node`, gid-0-writable state dirs). Rejected: `src/config/io.write-safety.ts` force-chmods the state dir back to `0700` on every config write when `configDir === stateDir`, which Compose always makes true; and it would not fix `~/.cache` in the `-browser` image or `~/.config`, both baked `0755`.
- **Build-arg uid.** Rejected: unusable with the published images.
- **Status quo (chown the host directories).** Already documented; it is precisely the case that fails here.

### Impact

Operators on any host with a non-1000 uid can run the published image against their own directories without host-side `sudo`, without rebuilding, and without a root process in the container. Nothing changes for existing deployments, which keep resolving to `1000:1000`.

### Evidence/examples

Measured in a container as uid 1026 with no `/etc/passwd` entry:

- `os.userInfo()` throws `uv_os_get_passwd returned ENOENT`, but every reachable call site in the Gateway is guarded, so this degrades rather than fails.
- `ssh -V` fails with `No user exists for uid 1026`, so the ssh sandbox backend and node pairing over ssh are genuinely unavailable at a custom uid. This is a real limitation to document, not to hide.
- `mkdir /home/node/.cache` fails with `EACCES`, which is what the cache redirection above fixes.

Prior art for the same shape: Grafana's numeric `USER` plus documented `--user "$(id -u)"`, and the Podman quadlet already shipped in this repo.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this myself

### Additional information

Deliberately out of scope: these variables are inert under Kubernetes, where `scripts/k8s/manifests/deployment.yaml` pins `runAsUser`/`runAsGroup` directly.

`wsl --list --verbose`

Windows reported:

`Windows Subsystem for Linux has no installed distributions.`

I am not sure whether WSL is required for my OpenClaw setup, but I wanted to include this information in case it is relevant.

## My Main Concern

My biggest concern is that OpenClaw appeared to work initially but then stopped working the following day.

After that, I spent around **8 hours continuously trying to fix the problem**.

During that time, I tried:

1. OpenClaw Home Hub
2. Ollama

* Multiple OpenClaw installations
* Old configuration files
* Conflicting AI configurations
* Background OpenClaw processes
* Gateway problems
* The failed AI access test
* The locked SQLite file
* Missing dependencies such as WSL

3. What is the recommended and correct method for installing OpenClaw on Windows?

I have already spent a significant amount of time trying to solve this myself, so I would really appreciate guidance from someone who understands the OpenClaw installation and setup process.

issues.body:
## Summary

`tools.message.crossContext.marker` is documented and defaulted on, and `src/infra/outbound/outbound-policy.ts` declares eight message actions that must carry the `[from {channel}]` origin marker when an agent sends into a conversation other than the one it is bound to. The marker helper is only ever invoked on two of those eight paths. Content forwarded out of conversation A with `reply`, `sendWithEffect`, `sendAttachment`, `upload-file`, `thread-reply` or `sticker` lands in conversation B with no indication that it came from somewhere else.

This is a disclosure and provenance defect, not data loss. Delivery succeeds; what is missing is the origin label the marker policy exists to attach.

## Environment

- Commit: `3a54b13977eb4078d470426c4522e0e655b9ee93` (pinned worktree the proof was produced on)
- Also current on `origin/main` `debd174b3af4da4c2ca0b18bab9f50f4c598cc9d`, and on the intermediate `71e436920cc9e4e3f2ff057b86679c6ed39c5115`. `git diff` over `src/infra/outbound/` between the pinned commit and both later commits is empty, so the cited lines are byte-identical on all three.
- Surface: message tool outbound action runner, all channels that route actions through `dispatchChannelMessageAction`

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure an agent bound to conversation `C12345678` on any channel whose plugin implements `actions.handleAction` (leave `tools.message.crossContext.marker` at its default, enabled).
2. Have the agent call the message tool with `action: "send"`, `to: "C99999999"`, `message: "secret cross-context reply body"`. The delivered text is prefixed with the origin marker.
3. Repeat with `action: "reply"` and the same `to` and `message`. The delivered text has no prefix.
4. Same outcome for `thread-reply`, `sendAttachment` and `sticker`.

## Expected

Every action listed in `CONTEXT_MARKER_ACTIONS` carries the origin marker when the outbound target is not the bound conversation, so a reader in the destination conversation can see the content was forwarded from elsewhere.

## Actual

Only `send` and `poll` carry it. The other six deliver the raw body.

## Root cause

`src/infra/outbound/outbound-policy.ts:54-63` declares the policy table. All eight entries:

```ts
const CONTEXT_MARKER_ACTIONS = new Set<ChannelMessageActionName>([
  "send",
  "poll",
  "reply",
  "sendWithEffect",
  "sendAttachment",
  "upload-file",
  "thread-reply",
  "sticker",
]);
```

`shouldApplyCrossContextMarker` (`outbound-policy.ts:351`) is the only consumer of that set, and it is reached only from `applyMessageCrossContextMarker` (`src/infra/outbound/message-action-execution.ts:233`). A repo-wide grep finds exactly two invocations of that helper:

```
$ grep -rn "applyMessageCrossContextMarker" --include=*.ts . | grep -v node_modules
src/infra/outbound/message-action-execution.ts:233:export async function applyMessageCrossContextMarker(params: {
src/infra/outbound/message-action-execution.ts:448:  await applyMessageCrossContextMarker({
src/infra/outbound/message-action-send.ts:40:  applyMessageCrossContextMarker,
src/infra/outbound/message-action-send.ts:255:        applyMessageCrossContextMarker({
```

- `message-action-send.ts:255` passes a hardcoded `action: "send"`, so it can only ever satisfy the `send` entry.
- `message-action-execution.ts:448` sits inside `executeMessagePoll` (declared at `:431`, `const action: ChannelMessageActionName = "poll"`), so it can only ever satisfy the `poll` entry.

`src/infra/outbound/message-action-runner.ts:707-713` routes `send` to `executeMessageSend`, `poll` to `executeMessagePoll`, and everything else to `executeMessagePlugin`. `executeMessagePlugin` (`message-action-execution.ts:548` onward) is therefore the sole handler for `reply`, `sendWithEffect`, `sendAttachment`, `upload-file`, `thread-reply` and `sticker`. Reading `:548-760`, it applies citation-marker hygiene to `params.message`, resolves outbound thread metadata, then goes straight to `executeGatewayAction` or `dispatchChannelMessageAction`. It never calls the marker helper, and nothing else on that path consults `CONTEXT_MARKER_ACTIONS`.

So the declared policy covers eight actions and the implementation covers two. The gap is a missing call site.

An initial field-mismatch theory, that the marker was written to a payload field the plugin path does not read, was investigated and disproved: `applyCrossContextMessageDecoration` (`message-action-execution.ts:204-230`) assigns the decorated text back to `params.message`, which is exactly the field `executeMessagePlugin` hygienes at `:583` and hands to the plugin as `ctx.params.message`. When the helper is invoked on that path the marker does show up in the delivered body, which the patched run below confirms. The two covered actions differ from the six uncovered ones only in whether the helper is called at all.

Suggested direction: apply the marker once inside the shared execution path, so every action in `CONTEXT_MARKER_ACTIONS` inherits it, rather than at individual call sites that each have to remember to opt in. As long as coverage is opt-in per handler, the declared table and the real behavior can drift again the next time an action is added.

## Age

This is longstanding and predates the outbound runner split. `git blame` dates the table entries to `09bed2ccdec8` (2026-01-17, `send`/`poll`/`thread-reply`/`sticker`), `1eab8fa9b03c` (2026-01-19, `reply`/`sendWithEffect`/`sendAttachment`) and `432d5f863cfd` (2026-03-26, `upload-file`). The runner split is `627e5bb06306cc5218e7e64247626456e8767881` (2026-08-09, "refactor(outbound): split message action runner by concept (#121434)"). At its parent commit the helper was named `maybeApplyCrossContextMarker` and had the same two call sites, in the pre-split `message-action-runner.ts` at `:1366` (the `send` path) and `:1749` (the `poll` path). The split moved the code without changing coverage.

## Novelty

Closest neighbors, none of which cover this:

- #93358 "fix(outbound): guard cross-context message mutations" (merged 2026-06-15). Added `edit`/`delete`/`pin`/`unpin` to `CONTEXT_GUARDED_ACTIONS` and wrote the comment above `CONTEXT_MARKER_ACTIONS` explaining why mutations stay out of the marker set. It is about which actions are denied, not about which ones actually get a marker, and it left the two call sites untouched.
- #119845 "fix(feishu): honor cross-context limits for message mutations" (merged). Channel-specific enforcement of the same guard set, again on the deny side.
- #1751 "fix(bluebubbles): ... prevent internal IDs leaking in cross-context prefix" (merged). Fixes what the origin label renders as on a path where the marker is already applied.
- #3587 / #1892 "fix(message): disable cross-context marker by default" (both closed). About the default value of `marker.enabled`, not about coverage.
- #123471 "message tool: any agent can send as another agent's channel account". Different defect, sender identity rather than origin labeling.

Searched: cross context marker, applyMessageCrossContextMarker, CONTEXT_MARKER_ACTIONS, cross-context provenance, message action provenance marker, marker missing reply, cross-context marker reply, sendAttachment cross-context, thread-reply marker, outbound marker not applied, message-action-execution. Nothing open or merged addresses the missing call site on the plugin action path.

## Real behavior proof
Behavior addressed: the declared cross-context origin marker reaches only two of the eight actions that declare it, so forwarded content arrives unlabeled.
Real environment tested: real `runMessageAction` outbound runner driven end to end at commit 3a54b13977eb4078d470426c4522e0e655b9ee93, with a registered channel plugin whose `actions.handleAction` and `outbound.sendText` record the body the channel transport was handed; policy, routing, normalization, threading and dispatch all ran as shipped.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: `./node_modules/.bin/vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.infra.config.ts --no-coverage src/infra/outbound/zz-xcontext-marker-repro.test.ts` (throwaway harness, not committed; it only registers the channel plugin and records what the transport receives), driving six actions with `toolContext.currentChannelId = "C12345678"`, `to = "C99999999"` and `message = "secret cross-context reply body"`; then the same harness re-run against a tree carrying a candidate marker call inside the shared plugin execution path.
Evidence after fix:
```
# OBSERVED (buggy, origin/main 3a54b13977eb4078d470426c4522e0e655b9ee93)
send -> to=C99999999 body="[from C12345678] secret cross-context reply body"
reply -> to=C99999999 body="secret cross-context reply body"
poll -> to=C99999999 body="[from C12345678] secret cross-context reply body"
thread-reply -> to=C99999999 body="secret cross-context reply body"
sendAttachment -> to=C99999999 body="secret cross-context reply body"
sticker -> to=C99999999 body="secret cross-context reply body"

# EXPECTED (same inputs, candidate marker call added to the shared plugin path)
send -> to=C99999999 body="[from C12345678] secret cross-context reply body"
reply -> to=C99999999 body="[from C12345678] secret cross-context reply body"
poll -> to=C99999999 body="[from C12345678] secret cross-context reply body"
thread-reply -> to=C99999999 body="[from C12345678] secret cross-context reply body"
sendAttachment -> to=C99999999 body="[from C12345678] secret cross-context reply body"
sticker -> to=C99999999 body="[from C12345678] secret cross-context reply body"
```
Observed result after fix: on unmodified main the origin label reaches only `send` and `poll`, while `reply`, `thread-reply`, `sendAttachment` and `sticker` hand the channel transport the bare forwarded body, and adding a single marker call on the shared plugin path restores the label for all six.
What was not tested: only four of the six uncovered actions were driven end to end; `sendWithEffect` and `upload-file` were confirmed by routing and code reading, not by a live delivery. No real provider was contacted, so per-channel rendering of the label and any channel that overrides `buildCrossContextPresentation` were not exercised. The gateway-delivery branch of `executeGatewayAction` was not driven; the local dispatch branch was. No judgement is offered on whether the six uncovered actions should be in the declared set or whether the set should shrink.

## Summary

Phone Talk (Android app, realtime) delegates substantive requests through the `openclaw_agent_consult` tool, whose allowlist is a closed three-value tool policy: `safe-read-only` (default), `owner`, `none`. In 2026.9.4 the config schema only exposes `toolPolicy` for Discord voice (`channels.discord.voice.realtime.toolPolicy`) — app Talk sessions have no equivalent key, so consults from phone Talk are always read-only (read, web_search, web_fetch, memory_search, memory_get). No exec, no subagent spawn, even for the owner.

## Request

Expose `toolPolicy` (or an equivalent consult-policy config) for app Talk sessions, e.g. `talk.realtime.toolPolicy: "owner"`. The consult tool already implements the `owner` policy (no allowlist restriction; the delegated agent turn gets the full toolset subject to normal exec approval/sandbox policy) — the plumbing exists in `src/talk/agent-consult-tool.ts`, it's just unwired on this surface.

## Use case

Voice-driven host commands while away from a screen: "restart the searxng service," "what's the gateway load," "kick off the backup." Today these all dead-end at the read-only consult boundary. Normal exec approval policy still applies to the delegated turn, so the security story matches a text session.

## Environment

- Gateway: OpenClaw 2026.9.4 (3a9d69d)
- Client: OpenClaw Android app on Pixel 9 (GrapheneOS)
- Realtime provider: google

## Related

- #130094 — exec blocked by voice confirmation gate in Browser Talk (same underlying ask: real tool use from voice, different code path)
- #133844 — Gateway-controlled native realtime for thin audio clients
- #71849 — realtime consult speed/fragility

issues.body:
## Summary

Codex app-server stores under `agents/<id>/agent/codex-home/` grow without bound and have no retention mechanism. On this install they reached **13 GB across 14 agents** in roughly two weeks, growing **~400 MB/day**. About **97% of the volume is image payloads** (browser-automation screenshots and generated images) embedded in thread history and logs.

`session.maintenance` — including `coldStorage`, `pruneAfter` and `maxDiskBytes` — does not cover these files. Per the docs it manages "SQLite session rows, SQLite transcript rows, archive artifacts, and trajectory sidecars" for OpenClaw's own session store, which on this install is only 0.6 GB. The 13 GB sits entirely outside its reach.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.9.4, Node 26.8.1, macOS 27.0 (Mac mini M4)
- 14 agents, Codex runtime via ChatGPT OAuth
- One agent (`lyra`) runs a daily browser-automation task (Google Flow) and accounts for 5.2 GB alone

## Measurements

`agents/lyra/agent/codex-home/thread_history_1.sqlite` — 711 MB:

| item_type | count | size |
|---|---|---|
| `userMessage` | 889 | **594 MB** |
| `imageGeneration` | 31 | 88 MB |
| `commandExecution` | 1567 | 12 MB |
| `dynamicToolCall` | 1682 | 5 MB |
| `reasoning` | 3589 | ~0 MB |

512 of the 889 `userMessage` items contain image data. Average item is 685 KB, largest is 4 MB. For contrast, 3589 reasoning blocks take almost no space — text is negligible.

`agents/lyra/agent/codex-home/logs_2.sqlite` — 778 MB, 175,424 rows:

| target | rows | size |
|---|---|---|
| `codex_core::session::handlers` | 1,914 | **603 MB** |
| everything else | 173,510 | ~61 MB |

751 of those 1,914 rows contain `image`, 220 contain `base64`. Largest single log row is 5 MB.

## Why age-based pruning does not help

No row in `logs_2` is older than 14 days — the oldest is 10 days old. The database is large because of **payload size**, not history depth. Pruning by age would reclaim little and the size returns within a week.

## What appears to be missing

1. **No retention policy for `codex-home` stores.** `session.maintenance` does not reach them, and no separate setting was found in the docs or in the runtime.
2. **Image payloads are stored inline and kept indefinitely.** OpenClaw's own compaction already treats images as droppable — it substitutes `[image data omitted from summary input]` when summarizing. The same idea does not seem to apply to what is persisted on disk.
3. **Logging persists full payloads.** A single log row reaching 5 MB suggests image data is written into `codex_core::session::handlers` records, not just referenced.

## Suggestions

- A retention/size policy for `codex-home` equivalent to `session.maintenance` (age, disk budget, or both).
- Strip or externalize image payloads from **inactive** thread items once the session is no longer live, keeping a marker — the same treatment compaction already applies.
- Cap or elide large binary payloads in log records.

Happy to provide additional measurements from this install, or to test a fix.
