issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

In containerized deployments without systemd, tools.exec.security=ask issues a Telegram approval card but executes the pending command ~3.5s later regardless of the approval outcome, instead of blocking until approved or denied.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start the gateway (ghcr.io/openclaw/openclaw:2026.7.1-2) in a Docker container without
   systemd/launchd, with tools.exec.security=allowlist, ask=on-miss,
   approvals.exec.mode=targets (Telegram DM routing).
2. Trigger an exec command that misses the allowlist, e.g. `mkdir -p /tmp/inline-button-test`.
3. An approval card is issued via Telegram (observed: card `eeff8125-df93-4fe4-85d7-41671515a74b`
   at 2026-08-17T12:39:10Z), with Allow Once/Allow Always/Deny options and a 30m expiry.
4. Do not respond to the card. Check the filesystem for the command's side effect immediately.

### Expected behavior

In the same deployment (same image, same config) with tools.exec.security=deny instead of
ask, an equivalent unmatched command (`mkdir -p /tmp/deny-canary-test`) is blocked
synchronously and never executes ("Exec denied (user-denied)", directory never created,
confirmed via stat/ls). This confirms blocking is achievable in this deployment. ask mode
should likewise block execution pending the approval decision or TTL expiry, consistent with
the card's own presented semantics (expiry countdown, pending response options).

### Actual behavior

The command executed 3.5 seconds after the approval card was issued — directory birth time
(via `stat`) was 2026-08-17T12:39:13.524Z, vs. card issued at 12:39:10Z. No approval or
denial record for this card exists in the session log or openclaw.sqlite-wal at the time of
execution (grep confirmed). The command ran regardless of the pending/unresolved approval
state.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.1-2

### Operating system

Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm), arm64, kernel 6.12.76-linuxkit (Docker on macOS host)

### Install method

docker

### Model

zai/glm-5.2 (agents.defaults.model.primary — likely irrelevant to this bug, which reproduces at the exec-approval gateway layer independent of model)

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw -> zai (Z.ai) GLM-5.2 (no separate provider field in config; provider is embedded in the model spec)

### Additional provider/model setup details

Model: zai/glm-5.2 via agents.defaults.model.primary (no per-agent override for main).
Provider is embedded in the model spec (zai = Z.ai); no separate provider field exists in
config. Not relevant to root cause — the reported bug is at the exec-approval gateway layer,
independent of model/provider.

### Logs

```shell
Approval card raw text (issued 2026-08-17T12:39:10Z, id eeff8125-df93-4fe4-85d7-41671515a74b):
"Approval required. Run: /approve eeff8125-df93-4fe4-85d7-41671515a74b allow-once
Pending command: mkdir -p /tmp/inline-button-test
Other options: /approve eeff8125-df93-4fe4-85d7-41671515a74b allow-always /
/approve eeff8125-df93-4fe4-85d7-41671515a74b deny
Host: gateway / CWD: ~/.openclaw/workspace / Expires in: 30m"

grep -A2 -B2 "eeff8125" openclaw.sqlite-wal: no approval/denial record found at time of
execution (12:39:13.524Z).

Workaround confirmed (deny mode canary test, same command shape):
"Exec denied (user-denied)" — directory never created (verified via stat/ls).

openclaw gateway restart failure (separate finding, same environment):
"Gateway service disabled. / Start with: openclaw gateway install /
systemctl --user start openclaw-gateway.service / systemd user services are unavailable;
install/enable systemd or run the gateway under your supervisor. / If you're in a container,
run the gateway in the foreground instead of `openclaw gateway`."
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

Affected: Any OpenClaw deployment using tools.exec.security=ask as an approval-gated
security control — verified in a Docker container without systemd/launchd
(ghcr.io/openclaw/openclaw:2026.7.1-2). Not tested on systemd/launchd-supervised hosts, so
scope beyond this environment is unconfirmed.
Severity: Critical — the approval gate provides no actual access control. A command executes
regardless of whether it is approved, denied, or left unresolved, so ask mode grants no
protection beyond the allowlist itself.
Frequency: Deterministic in the tested case (1/1) — reproduced with exact timestamps (card
issued 12:39:10Z, exec completed 12:39:13.524Z, no approval record at execution time). Not
yet tested across repeated trials.
Consequence: Any exec command missing the allowlist executes immediately regardless of the
human approval decision, defeating the purpose of approval-gated exec as a safety control.
Confirmed workaround: tools.exec.security=deny blocks correctly and synchronously, but
sacrifices ask mode's per-request approval flexibility for an allow/deny-only model.

### Additional information

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO regarding last-known-good version — no evidence was collected that ask mode
ever correctly blocked exec in any prior release; this may not be a regression.

Grounded additional context: switching tools.exec.security from ask to deny in the same
deployment (same version, same config) blocks an equivalent command synchronously and
correctly (canary-tested: "Exec denied (user-denied)", directory never created). This confirms
the underlying blocking mechanism works for deny but not for ask.

### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

With channels.imessage.groupPolicy set to "allowlist" and both channels.imessage.allowFrom and groupAllowFrom empty ([]), the agent still processed inbound group messages and sent live responses in multiple group chats, including a group unrelated to any business context and a private family group.

Expected: per docs and the gateway's own startup warning ("Every inbound group message will be dropped"), messages should have been dropped with no session created.

Actual: the agent created a live session in group chat "imessage:group:1870" and, when an NVIDIA API call failed with a 503, sent the raw error text ("The AI service is temporarily overloaded. Please try again in a moment.") into that group as if it were a normal reply. Separately, in an unrelated private family group, the agent responded to an unrelated question with a generic AI disclaimer.

Reproduction evidence:
- Log: lane=session:agent:main:imessage:group:1870 error="FailoverError: The AI service is temporarily overloaded..."
- openclaw config get channels.imessage.allowFrom → []
- openclaw config get channels.imessage.groupPolicy → allowlist
- openclaw config get channels.imessage.groupAllowFrom → Config path not found

Impact: raw internal error strings are surfaced as message content to real external contacts with no indication it's automated. Group allowlist protection is not enforced consistently. Affects any group the account's iMessage number is in, not just business-context groups.

Suggested fix: (1) enforce the group allowlist check consistently for all inbound group triggers; (2) never surface raw provider error strings as deliverable message content to any external channel — log/route those to a private admin channel only.

Environment: OpenClaw 2026.7.1-2 (build 0790d9f), macOS, iMessage channel plugin, nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Set channels.imessage.groupPolicy to "allowlist" and leave channels.imessage.allowFrom and groupAllowFrom empty ([]).
2. Start the gateway and let it run with an iMessage number that is a participant in one or more group chats.
3. Wait for API errors or unrelated messages to occur in a group chat.
4. Observe the agent creates a session and sends a reply into the group (either a normal reply or, on API failure, the raw error text), despite no allowlist entries existing for that group or sender.

### Expected behavior

Per documentation and the gateway's own startup log warning ("groupPolicy=allowlist ... no group sender allowlist is configured ... Every inbound group message will be dropped"), no session should be created and no message should be sent for any group when allowFrom and groupAllowFrom are both empty.

### Actual behavior

The agent created a live session in group chat "imessage:group:1870" despite empty allowFrom/groupAllowFrom, and when an NVIDIA API call failed with a 503, it sent the raw error text ("The AI service is temporarily overloaded. Please try again in a moment.") into that group as a normal-looking reply. Separately, in an unrelated private family group chat, the agent responded to an unrelated question with a generic AI-assistant disclaimer.

Evidence:
- Log: lane=session:agent:main:imessage:group:1870 error="FailoverError: The AI service is temporarily overloaded. Please try again in a moment."
- openclaw config get channels.imessage.allowFrom -> []
- openclaw config get channels.imessage.groupPolicy -> allowlist
- openclaw config get channels.imessage.groupAllowFrom -> Config path not found

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.1-2 (build 0790d9f)

### Operating system

macOS (host: MacBookPro / Coens-MacBook-Pro)

### Install method

npm install -g openclaw@latest

### Model

nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b

### Provider / routing chain

nvidia provider, openai-completions API, direct to https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1/chat/completions, no proxy, no fallback model configured (fallbackConfigured: false)

### Additional provider/model setup details

Single NVIDIA API key/profile configured (profileId sha256:354ea9687bc3). No per-agent model overrides for the affected sessions. iMessage channel plugin (imsg) reading from local Messages database. Gateway run as a macOS LaunchAgent with KeepAlive: true.

### Logs

```shell
{"subsystem":"gateway/channels/imessage"}: embedded_run_agent_end, isError:true, error:"The AI service is temporarily overloaded. Please try again in a moment.", failoverReason:"overloaded", model:"nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b", providerRuntimeFailureKind:"timeout"

lane task error: lane=session:agent:main:imessage:group:1870 durationMs=1310 error="FailoverError: The AI service is temporarily overloaded. Please try again in a moment."

model_fallback_decision: decision:"candidate_failed", reason:"overloaded", status:503, fallbackConfigured:false, fallbackStepFinalOutcome:"chain_exhausted"

Config check at time of incident:
openclaw config get channels.imessage.allowFrom -> []
openclaw config get channels.imessage.groupPolicy -> allowlist
openclaw config get channels.imessage.groupAllowFrom -> Config path not found

Earlier startup log (same install, prior to incident) explicitly warned:
"imessage: groupPolicy=\"allowlist\" for account \"default\" but no group sender allowlist is configured (channels.imessage.groupAllowFrom, or its allowFrom fallback). Every inbound group message will be dropped."
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

Affected: any iMessage group chat the account's number participates in, including business-context groups and unrelated private/personal groups.
Severity: data/safety risk — raw internal error strings and unintended AI responses are delivered to real external contacts without disclosure that the message is automated, in contexts (private family group) with no relation to bot usage at all.
Frequency: observed at least twice across two separate group chats on the same day; underlying condition (empty allowlist not being enforced) is persistent, not a one-off, so recurrence should be expected whenever a group receives any inbound activity or an API call fails mid-session.
Consequence: unintended/confusing messages reaching real contacts and family members; reputational risk for business use; account owner had to manually leave affected group chats as the only reliable mitigation since config settings did not prevent the behavior.

issues.body:
## Problem

OpenClaw currently has a hard boundary around some protected config paths when changes are initiated from inside an agent session. That boundary is good in spirit: an agent should not be able to silently or autonomously grant itself more authority.

But the current implementation creates a sovereignty problem for owner-operated deployments: even when the human owner explicitly asks and confirms in chat, the agent has no valid approval path for protected changes such as enabling the `/mcp` command or registering an MCP server. The only available outcomes are:

1. refuse the owner request, or
2. bypass the OpenClaw config tool by raw-editing `openclaw.json`, which normalizes exactly the wrong precedent.

That is the wrong tradeoff. The system should preserve the guardrail while giving the owner a first-class, auditable approval path.

## Concrete example

Goal: register a locally installed MCP server after auditing/smoke-testing it.

The owner tried to run:

```text
/mcp set agentic-aqua={"command":"/Users/senemaro/.local/bin/aqua-mcp","args":[]}
```

OpenClaw replied:

```text
⚠️ /mcp is disabled. Set commands.mcp=true to enable.
```

The agent inspected the schema and confirmed:

```text
commands.mcp: boolean
Allow /mcp chat command to manage OpenClaw MCP server config under mcp.servers (default: false).
```

Then the agent attempted the sanctioned config path:

```json
{"commands":{"mcp":true}}
```

Gateway refused:

```text
gateway config.patch cannot change protected config paths: commands.mcp
```

This left no legitimate agent-mediated owner approval flow. The owner explicitly authorized the change, but OpenClaw still forced the choice between human manual editing and agent-side bypass.

## Why this matters

This is not a request to let agents freely self-escalate.

It is the opposite: owner-approved escalation should be explicit, structured, logged, and harder to confuse with autonomous agent behavior.

Right now, the hard block makes the safe path unavailable. A capable owner can still edit the file directly, but then OpenClaw loses the chance to:

- show the exact diff before approval,
- require an explicit human confirmation gesture,
- restart/reload safely,
- record an audit trail,
- distinguish owner intent from agent initiative,
- apply extra checks for dangerous MCP servers or command flags.

For local-first/open-source deployments, sovereignty means the owner can authorize changes to their own machine without teaching the agent to step around the runtime boundary.

## Current implementation clue

The gateway tool appears to allow only a small allowlist of config paths for agent-side mutation and rejects others as protected.

Observed in the installed build:

```ts
const ALLOWED_GATEWAY_CONFIG_PATHS = [
  "agents.defaults.systemPromptOverride",
  "agents.defaults.promptOverlays",
  "agents.defaults.model",
  "agents.defaults.thinkingDefault",
  "agents.defaults.subagents.thinking",
  "agents.defaults.reasoningDefault",
  "agents.defaults.fastModeDefault",
  "agents.list[].id",
  "agents.list[].systemPromptOverride",
  "agents.list[].model",
  "agents.list[].thinkingDefault",
  "agents.list[].subagents.thinking",
  "agents.list[].reasoningDefault",
  "agents.list[].fastModeDefault",
  "channels.*.requireMention",
  "channels.*.*.requireMention",
  "channels.*.*.*.requireMention",
  "channels.*.*.*.*.requireMention",
  "channels.*.*.*.*.*.requireMention",
  "messages.visibleReplies",
  "messages.groupChat.visibleReplies"
];
```

And:

```ts
if (disallowedPaths.length > 0) {
  throw new Error(`gateway ${params.action} cannot change protected config paths: ${disallowedPaths.join(", ")}`);
}
```

That hard error is the core UX/security problem: it treats all protected edits as impossible from the agent path, even with live owner confirmation.

## Proposed fix: owner-approved protected config changes

Add a first-class approval flow for protected config mutations instead of hard-failing immediately.

Suggested behavior:

1. Agent calls `gateway config.patch` or a new action such as `gateway config.propose`.
2. Gateway computes the exact changed paths and classifies risk:
   - normal allowlisted path → current behavior
   - protected path → requires owner approval
   - dangerous path/flag → requires stronger approval or remains blocked depending on policy
3. Gateway returns an approval card to the current human/operator surface showing:
   - exact config path(s), e.g. `commands.mcp`
   - old value and new value
   - full JSON patch/diff
   - risk label and explanation
   - whether restart is required
   - requesting agent/session identity
4. Human explicitly approves via the native approval UI or an owner-only command.
5. Gateway applies the change itself, writes an audit record, and restarts/hot-reloads as needed.

## Specific MCP handling

For MCP-related paths, add extra review fields:

- command path
- args
- environment variables/secrets referenced
- cwd
- whether command is absolute or PATH-resolved
- whether executable exists
- package provenance if known
- tool list if the server can be smoke-tested before enabling
- warning if tools include destructive/financial actions

Example approvals that should be possible:

```json
{"commands":{"mcp":true}}
```

and later:

```json
{
  "mcp": {
    "servers": {
      "agentic-aqua": {
        "command": "/Users/senemaro/.local/bin/aqua-mcp",
        "args": []
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## Safety requirements

This should not become a blanket escape hatch.

Recommended constraints:

- default deny for protected paths unless an explicit owner approval arrives;
- approvals expire quickly;
- approval must include exact patch hash/base config hash to prevent TOCTOU surprises;
- approval should be bound to the requesting session and patch contents;
- dangerous flags may require typed confirmation or config-level opt-in;
- all protected approvals should be logged in an audit trail;
- channel identity should matter: group chat confirmation should be treated differently from a local TUI or authenticated owner DM;
- optional config policy could disable this feature entirely for hosted/shared deployments.

## Why this is better than the current state

The current state is neither fully safe nor sovereign:

- It blocks legitimate owner-directed work through the sanctioned tool.
- It pressures users toward manual edits or alternate agents.
- It gives agents an incentive to consider raw file bypasses.
- It provides no structured diff, approval, or audit trail for the actual change.

A protected-edit approval flow would make the safe thing also the easy thing.

## Acceptance criteria

- An agent can propose a protected config change without applying it.
- The owner sees an exact diff and risk explanation.
- The owner can approve or deny through a first-class OpenClaw mechanism.
- Approved changes are applied by Gateway, not by raw agent file editing.
- The approval is logged with session/agent/path/old/new metadata.
- Existing hard-block behavior remains available via config policy for deployments that want it.
- The MCP registration flow works without requiring manual `openclaw.json` edits when owner approval is present.

issues.body:
## Summary

A plugin's `before_prompt_build` hook can return an unbounded `prependSystemContext` that core injects verbatim into `systemPrompt` with no cap or warning. A third-party plugin (context-mode) prepends its resume snapshot this way; in production it reached **824,170 chars**, making the first turn's `systemPrompt` **895,171 chars** and the model rejects the request ("Context overflow: prompt too large for the model. Try /reset…"). `/reset` doesn't help because the payload comes from the plugin's store on every fresh session.

Measured via the `llm_input` hook:

| turn | systemPrompt | result |
|---|---|---|
| 1st after gateway restart / session reset | 895,171 chars (70,969 baseline + 824,170 plugin injection + 32 glue) | rejected |
| 2nd | 70,969 | normal |

## Why a core-side guard

Upstream bug is being reported to the plugin (context-mode `maxBytes` is documented as ignored), but core is the last line of defense: one misbehaving or verbose plugin can currently brick the first turn of every session with no signal about which payload is oversized. Suggest one or more of:

1. Cap (or soft-warn + truncate) `prependSystemContext` with a configurable budget, logging the contributing source and size;
2. Telemetry: when systemPrompt crosses a threshold (e.g. 50% of model window), log a breakdown of its parts — would have made this diagnosis instant.

The error message could also mention that the overflow came from injected context rather than chat history — "Try /reset" is misleading here since the payload is re-injected into fresh sessions.

Happy to provide the probe/diagnostics used.

issues.body:
## Summary

On a Telegram direct chat using the `claude-cli` runtime, earlier images keep being re-attached to later user turns that contain no media. Each new text-only message arrives with an "Image turn" block plus `@~/.openclaw-cli-images/<sha>.jpg` references to images from much earlier in the conversation. The only workaround is `/new`, which throws away the session context.

This looks related to #46655 (closed as not reproducible on Telegram). This report is for the claude-cli image-turn path, not the debouncer.

## Environment

- OpenClaw **2026.9.3**, and still present after updating to **2026.10.4 (383c124)**, gateway restarted
- Linux (Arch), systemd user gateway
- Channel: Telegram, direct chat (`chat_type: direct`)
- Runtime: `claude-cli` (Claude Code backend)

## Observed

1. The user sent a PNG screenshot as a **document** (Telegram file, not a compressed photo) at about 06:14.
2. Every later user turn for about 7 hours, mostly plain text, logged the same resize for that image:
   `[agents/tool-images] Image resized to fit limits: 2048x1152px 1.46MB -> 104.0KB (-93%)`
   That's 30+ turns in a row.
3. Sending a real photo did not clear it. The new photo was attached too, and the stale one came along with it.
4. Updating 9.3 → 10.4 and restarting the gateway did not clear it.
5. Later, the "stuck" set changed to two other images, and those now repeat on every turn:
   - a 1200x675 screenshot the user sent at about 13:53 (again as a PNG document)
   - a 90x1200 image that matches the aspect ratio of an image the **assistant itself sent** earlier as outbound `MEDIA:` (a 390x5193 full-page screenshot). So outbound assistant media seems able to come back in as user-turn images.

   Log lines on every text-only turn since then:
   ```
   [agents/tool-images] Image resized to fit limits: 2048x1152px 1.46MB -> 104.0KB (-93%)
   [agents/tool-images] Image resized to fit limits: 153x2037px 100.3KB -> 45.5KB (-54.6%)
   ```
   The user turn carries an `Image turn` context block with a new `turnKey` each time, plus `@/home/<user>/.openclaw-cli-images/<sha>.jpg` lines for the same two hashes.

## Expected

An image turn should only include media attached to the current inbound message, or to an explicit reply target. Neither earlier inbound documents nor the assistant's own outbound media should reappear on unrelated later turns.

## Impact

- The model treats the stale images as new input every turn. It wastes tokens and confuses replies ("the image you sent is X").
- The only fix is `/new`, which loses the long session's context. That's costly for long working sessions.

## Guesses (unverified)

- The selection of "conversation context" images for the claude-cli image turn may pull from recent transcript history, including assistant outbound media, instead of only the current message.
- PNG-as-document inbound may skip the cleanup that photo inbound gets.

I can provide more gateway log excerpts if useful. I haven't attached session data because it's private.

issues.body:
# Gateway restart sometimes hangs 30+ minutes to 2 hours on Windows multi-agent installs (2026.9.8)

## Environment
- OpenClaw 2026.9.8 (fc23bc8), Node 24.19.0, win32 x64, Windows 11, Ryzen 7 5700G (16 logical threads)
- Two gateway installs on one machine, each its own state dir and Windows Scheduled Task:
  - **Echo** (port 18789): agents `echo` (OpenAI `gpt-5.6-luna` primary, `gpt-5.6-terra` fallback, embedded runtime) and `echo-gemma` (local Ollama model, Gemma 4 E4B quantized GGUF); plus `main` and `echo-dreaming` agent databases
  - **Elias** (port 18790): agent `elias` (OpenAI `gpt-5.6-luna` primary, `gpt-5.6-terra` fallback, embedded runtime); plus `echo` and `echo-dreaming` agent databases
- Upgrade path: 2026.9.4 -> 2026.9.6 -> 2026.9.8, via `openclaw update repair`
- File paths below use `C:\Users\<user>\...` in place of the actual account name.

## Symptom
- Restart of a gateway with ~6 months of agent history takes about 2 hours before it answers the connectivity probe. Earlier restarts on 2026.9.4 and 2026.9.6 took a few minutes.
- The gateway process runs at a steady ~1 core (0.99 CPU-seconds per wall-second, 16 logical cores available), so it's CPU-bound, not waiting.
- Provider endpoints respond quickly (local Ollama ~3 ms; OpenAI ~0.2 s), and the gateway holds only a couple of network connections. Network is not the bottleneck.
- The log reports: `prepared model runtime startup degraded after 120000ms (workspace plugins; agent echo); still acquiring agents: echo, echo-gemma; acquisition continues in the background`

## Measured boot durations (2026.9.8, from process start to `gateway ready` in the log)
- 2026-10-04 17:57 -> 20:08 CDT: 131 min
- 2026-10-04 20:23 -> 22:25 CDT: 122 min
- Earlier boot (13:33 -> 13:38 CDT, approximate start): 6 min
- Starts and ready events are paired by timestamp and may be off by a few minutes; the 2026.9.4 baseline is not in surviving logs.
- Clean profile rebuild (`echo98`, see below), three consecutive boots: 3553 s, 3498 s, 3550 s (~58-59 min each), with no meaningful variance despite a clean stop and a fresh plugin cache between runs.

## Upgrade path (both installs, Windows)
- 2026.9.4 -> 2026.9.6 (2026-10-03): repair left plugin data upgrades "unfinished"; a later convergence step advanced the Discord plugin from its pinned 2026.8.2 to 2026.9.6 unprompted, wiping a hand-patch.
- 2026.9.6 -> 2026.9.8 (2026-10-04): repair took about 2 hours on the main Echo install (14:17 to 16:18 CDT), with the convergence step dominated by `incremental-vacuum`.
- Cron `DataCloneError` regression first seen in 9.6. Not yet re-tested on 9.8 (the isolated agentTurn jobs have not been run on 9.8).

## Data size (agent SQLite)
- echo / echo-gemma agent DB: 135 MB / 108 MB
- Elias main agent DB: 180 MB
- Elias main `transcript_events`: 16,620 rows across 14 sessions (about 52 MB of text)
- echo-gemma `memory_index_chunks`: 3,084 rows (+ FTS, 5,491 embedding cache rows)

## Related slow SQLite operations seen during `openclaw update repair`
- `slow SQLite transaction hold ... operation=incremental-vacuum elapsedMs=1883`
- Repeated `Shared-state WAL maintenance failed ... undergoing offline maintenance; retry when it finishes.`
- Doctor step (`finalize:targetConfigConvergence`) ran about 104 minutes for Echo and about 2 hours total for `update repair`.

## Root cause evidence, part 1 (2026-10-05 tests on a fresh 2026.9.8 install with copied live state)
- Clean install: ready in about 24 s.
- Copied Echo-Gemma agent DB (108 MB): ready in about 23 s.
- Copied Elias main agent DB (166 MB): ready in about 24 s.
- Copied live state DB with cron tables (scheduler disabled): ready in about 10 min 13 s.
- Same state DB with three missing columns added by hand: ready in about 24 s.
- Schema diff vs canonical 2026.9.8 baseline: `subagent_runs` missing `controller_store_path` and `requester_store_path`; `worker_workspace_pending_results` missing `repository_workspace_id`. Logs show `SqliteSchemaMismatchError` during cron session publication. `openclaw database preflight` reports the schema version as exact (19 of 19), so the mismatch is missing columns, not a version number.
- `openclaw doctor --fix` on the drifted copy took 143 s, reported "Doctor finished with plugin load errors", and did NOT add the missing columns.
- Doctor refuses maintenance while the state database holds agent-database lease rows owned by a live gateway PID. Copies of live state carry those rows, so the test had to clear them first.

## Hypothesis (not yet verified)
- The prepared model catalog inventory appears to live only in memory (`previousInventory = params.inventoryOwner.catalogInventory`) and I did not find persistence in the prepared-model-runtime module, so each boot may rebuild the full catalog for each agent.
- This is inferred from reading `dist/prepared-model-runtime-*.mjs`; it has not been profiled.
- Note: the CPU-bound (~1 core, 0.99 CPU-s/wall-s) observation above was from a different boot than the zero-CPU hang documented below. Both are real, but they are not the same phenomenon; the install may hit either path depending on state.

## Root cause evidence, part 2 (2026-10-07, clean profile-based rebuild, CPU-sampled)
To rule out schema drift, unclean shutdowns, and stale plugin caches as the sole causes, a brand-new CLI-managed profile install (`openclaw --profile echo98`, port 18792, Discord disabled, isolated from the live gateways) was built from scratch: config regenerated by `openclaw setup --baseline`, agent and state SQLite databases snapshotted from the live install with `VACUUM INTO` (all pass `PRAGMA quick_check`), the known three-column schema drift fix applied, stale `agent_database_leases`/`state_leases` rows cleared, and the `npm` plugin cache deleted so plugins reinstall fresh under the new path. This is a managed service install (`gateway install`/`start`/`stop`), so `gateway stop --force` now exits cleanly in about 13 seconds — confirming non-default state dirs were the reason `gateway stop` couldn't manage the live installs, not an unrelated bug.

Despite all of that, three consecutive boots of this clean profile still took 3553 s, 3498 s, and 3550 s (all ~58-59 minutes) before the connectivity probe passed. This number is consistent across a clean stop, a clean npm cache, a schema-fixed DB, and no leases, which rules out every hypothesis above as the sole cause.

Log evidence from the third boot: the process logs `loading configuration…`, `resolving authentication…`, `starting...`, `shutdown budget at startup: ...` all within the same 2 seconds of process start, then produces **zero log output for the next ~57 minutes**, before resuming with ordinary secrets-resolution and plugin-load messages and reaching `gateway ready` about 20 seconds later.

A fourth boot was sampled directly (`Get-Process`, every 30 s, for the full window):
- `CPU` (seconds) stayed exactly flat at 10.203125 for the entire ~55-minute gap — the process did not consume CPU time while "hung".
- Thread count (13) and handle count (213) stayed constant the whole time — no handle leak, no thread storm.
- Working set fell steadily from 182 MB to 19 MB and stayed at 19 MB — consistent with Windows trimming the working set of an idle/blocked process, not with active computation.
- The probe then passed within about a minute of this flat period ending.

This rules out a busy loop or heavy computation (the earlier `prepared model runtime startup degraded after 120000ms` message and the catalog-rebuild hypothesis would predict CPU usage, not silence). It is consistent with the main thread blocked in a single native call — most plausibly a network request without a timeout (candidates present in config: `tavily`, `brave`, `google`, and Ollama model-capability probing) or a blocking filesystem call. Ruled out on this host: `O:` is a local NTFS disk (`DriveType=3`), not a network share, and Windows Defender real-time protection is disabled, so AV-filter-driver interference and SMB latency are unlikely explanations.

One plugin load error recurs across all three boots of the clean profile, even after deleting the profile's own `npm` folder: `codex failed during load ... EXDEV: cross-device link not permitted, link 'O:\openclaw\.openclaw-echo\npm\projects\openclaw-codex-...\...\codex-code-mode-host.exe' -> 'C:\Users\<user>\.openclaw-echo98\tmp\plugin-captures\...'`. This means some piece of plugin provenance metadata (not the `npm` folder itself, since it was deleted and rebuilt) still records the absolute path of the *original* install on `O:`, and the new install under `C:` tries to hardlink from it. This error resolves in under 20 seconds once plugin loading starts, so it is not the cause of the 57-minute gap, but it is itself a separate bug worth reporting: profile/install migrations cannot cleanly detach from the source install's recorded paths.

## Root cause evidence, part 3 (2026-10-07, full process dump during the hang)
A full memory dump (`procdump -ma`) was captured on the `echo98` profile about 2.5 minutes into a fifth boot, while still inside the silent window, and inspected with WinDbg (`~*k`). Findings:
- The main thread is blocked in `ntdll!NtRemoveIoCompletionEx` -> `KERNELBASE!GetQueuedCompletionStatusEx` -> `node!uv_run`. This is libuv's event loop sitting idle, waiting for the next timer or I/O completion — not computation, not a deadlock on a lock, and not a spin loop.
- Every other thread (3x `V8Worker`, 3x `libuv-worker`, 1x `DelayedTaskSchedulerWorker`, plus 2 generic worker-factory/thread-pool threads) is parked on `SleepConditionVariableCS` / `NtWaitForWorkViaWorkerFactory` — ordinary idle thread-pool threads with nothing queued.
- No thread is blocked in a network syscall, a file-lock wait, or a mutex wait on another process's handle. There is nothing to attach a filesystem or network explanation to; the process is doing *nothing* except waiting for the event loop's next scheduled wakeup.
- This means whatever causes the ~58-minute gap must be a timer or a pending async handle that was armed with a long duration very early in startup (right after `starting...`, before any other log line), and the gap ends when that timer/handle finally fires.
- The three measured boot times on this same clean profile (3553 s, 3498 s, 3550 s) cluster within 1.5% of each other and are all close to exactly one hour (3600 s). That consistency, combined with the idle-event-loop evidence, points at a fixed timeout constant (plausibly intended as milliseconds but applied as a larger unit, or an intentional but oversized retry/backoff ceiling) rather than network or disk variability, which would not produce boot times this tightly clustered.

## Root cause evidence, part 4 (2026-10-07, the slow boot is intermittent on the live installs)
An unrelated incident gave an unplanned data point. The live Echo and Elias gateways (the original installs on `O:`, not the `echo98` profile copy) were both force-killed by Windows Installer's Restart Manager (triggered by an attempted Node.js point-release upgrade, unrelated to OpenClaw) and had to be restarted from their scheduled tasks — the same kind of unclean process kill used throughout this investigation.

This time, both came back in under 35 seconds (Echo: 25s, Elias: 34s), not the 74 and 128 minutes measured on these same two installs two days earlier under what looks like an equivalent unclean-kill scenario (same machine, same installs, same schema-fixed state, same lease-clearing).

This means the multi-minute-to-multi-hour boot is **not consistently reproducible on the live installs**, even though it was **100% reproducible (3 of 3 runs, 3553s/3498s/3550s) on the from-scratch `echo98` profile** described above. Two explanations seem most likely and are not mutually exclusive:
1. Something only the `echo98` profile hits every time — most plausibly tied to the cross-device (`O:` to `C:`) plugin-capture path recorded in its plugin provenance metadata (see the `EXDEV` evidence above) — forces a slow path on every boot for that profile specifically, while the live installs (plugin source and capture destination both on `O:`) don't hit it.
2. Whatever causes the hang on the live installs depends on some other condition (time since last full capture rebuild, a cache validity window, directory bloat from the uncollected plugin-capture directories documented in #157989 and #162822) that was satisfied differently on the two occasions.
We did not have an opportunity to inspect the live installs' `tmp/plugin-captures` state at the moment of either the slow or the fast boot, so we can't yet say which.

## Root cause evidence, part 5 (2026-10-07, the fast boot was the anomaly, not the norm — and shutdown method correlates with it)
To check whether the ~30-second boot above was the new normal, the same two live installs were killed again (`taskkill /F`) and restarted the same way. Both reverted to the slow pattern: Elias 4955 s (~83 min), Echo 7571 s (~126 min) — consistent with the original 74/128-minute measurements, not the ~30-second one.

This leaves one clean, falsifiable difference between the one fast boot and every slow one observed in this investigation: **how the prior process was terminated.**
- Every slow boot followed a termination we performed directly: `taskkill /F`, or the CLI's own `gateway stop --force` (on the `echo98` profile, part 2 above). Despite the name, `--force` did not prevent the slow boot, so it does not appear to perform a graceful app-level shutdown either.
- The one fast boot (~30 s, part 4 above) followed Windows's Restart Manager terminating the process as part of an MSI install's file-in-use handling. Restart Manager is documented to request a graceful shutdown from applications before resorting to termination.

This fits the original working theory from early in this investigation (clean shutdown -> clean-close receipt -> fast next boot; unclean kill -> full integrity/rebuild path -> slow next boot), which we had set aside after the `echo98` profile stayed slow even after a `gateway stop --force`. The new data suggests `--force` (and plain `taskkill /F`) are not actually achieving a graceful shutdown, while something Restart Manager does — even though it still ends in the process exiting — is. **We do not have a way to invoke that same graceful path ourselves**; `gateway stop` without `--force` refuses to act on these non-default state dirs, and `--force` behaves like a kill as far as the next boot is concerned.

## What would help most (updated)
- A supported way to request a graceful gateway shutdown on a non-default state dir / profile, that actually achieves whatever Restart Manager achieved in part 5 above. Right now `gateway stop` refuses outright and `gateway stop --force` behaves like a kill for this purpose, so operators have no way to avoid the slow next boot on a planned restart.
- Given the stack-trace evidence above, what we need now is not a process dump (we have one) but a pointer into the source: where a long timer or long-lived async handle could be armed between process start and the first plugin/secrets log line, on a path gated by agent/plugin count (since clean single-agent fresh installs boot in ~24 s, and multi-agent installs consistently take ~58-59 min regardless of data size or drift).
- Confirmation of whether the prepared model catalog is meant to be persisted across restarts.
- Where plugin install provenance (the source path baked in for cross-device link/build steps) is stored, and whether there's a supported way to re-point or clear it when moving/copying an install to a new path.

## Related regression (separate, same version line)
- Isolated `agentTurn` cron jobs fail at setup with `DataCloneError: #<Object> could not be cloned` (source `cron-setup`) since 2026.9.6, on both installs, including jobs with clean history, for manual and scheduled runs.
- Not fixed or mentioned in the 9.7 or 9.8 release notes. Not yet tested on 9.8 for cron.

## Related issues
This appears to be the same general area (startup wall-time scaling badly with agent/plugin count on Windows) as several already-open reports, but none describe the specific zero-CPU idle-event-loop signature or the near-exactly-one-hour clustering documented in part 3 above:
- #152981 — startup hangs ~17 min at `sidecars.model-runtime`, multi-agent, but CPU-saturated (not idle) and ends in failure rather than resolving
- #155859 — startup wall-time scales with enabled plugin count; `discord` and `codex` are named as the largest contributors, which matches our plugin set
- #162211 — event loop blocked 40-200s with `active:0/waiting:0/queued:0` but near-100% CPU, causing a health-monitor restart loop
- #157545 — CLI commands and gateway startup taking 20-30+ minutes on 2026.9.6, described as event-loop/system overload (same reporter as #152981, same agent count)
- #157989 and #162822 — plugin source capture copies every file on every load with no reuse/hardlinking; this matches our `EXDEV` evidence in part 2 exactly (same `codex-code-mode-host.exe` capture path pattern), though it resolves in under 20s for us and is not the cause of the main hang

## Dependency versions (checked day of filing)
- `openclaw` (CLI/gateway): 2026.9.8 — current stable release (next, `2026.10.1-beta.1`, is a pre-release channel, not used here)
- `@openclaw/discord`, `@openclaw/codex`, `@openclaw/brave-plugin`, `@openclaw/tavily-plugin`: all 2026.9.8 — current
- `@openclaw/fs-safe` / `@openclaw/fs-safe-win32-x64-msvc`: 0.21.1 — pinned by `openclaw@2026.9.8`'s own `package.json`; not independently upgradable
- Node.js: 24.19.0 — the newest version available through this host's package manager (winget) for the LTS channel; nodejs.org has since published 24.21.0, which winget's manifest has not picked up yet

## Attached
- Payload-free diagnostics export: `O:\openclaw\.openclaw-echo\logs\support\openclaw-diagnostics-2026-10-05T11-56-08-031Z-17828.zip`
  - Note: its stability bundle is from a 2026-09-05 startup failure, not from the slow boot, so it does not show phase timings for the 2-hour boot.
- A full process dump captured during an active hang (`echo98-hang.dmp`, ~329 MB, 2026-10-07), available on request.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Crash (process/app exits or hangs)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

On an ARM64 Android/PRoot host, enabling the external plugin `context-mode` 1.0.169
makes gateway startup take ~200s instead of ~10-30s. The plugin's own code is not
slow: its `register()` runs in ~65ms. Timestamp instrumentation in the plugin entry
shows the gateway spends ~165-170s **before the plugin module is even evaluated**.

The HTTP server binds early but the gateway is not ready, so the Control UI appears
down for several minutes. This points at OpenClaw's external-plugin
load/source-capture path rather than the plugin itself.

### Steps to reproduce

1.Install OpenClaw 2026.10.4 and install `context-mode` from npm as an external
   plugin.
2. Enable it: `plugins.entries.context-mode.enabled=true`.
3. Restart the gateway service.
4. Measure the time until `http server listening` appears in the log, or until the
   Control UI becomes r

### Expected behavior

Gateway ready in roughly 10-30s, as it is with the plugin disabled.

### Actual behavior

Startup times observed across restarts with `context-mode` enabled:

```
195.8s, 232.9s, 197.2s, 205.3s, 203.8s, 203.4s
```

With `context-mode` disabled:

```
10.1s, 31.4s
```

During the stall the gateway process is alive and the HTTP listener is bound, but
readiness/WebSocket probes time out.

### OpenClaw version

2026.10.4

### Operating system

Linux6.2.1-PRoot-Distro (arm64)process.platform=Linux

### Install method

npm global

### Model

默认主模型deepseek/deepseek-V4-flash;图像模型deepseek/deepseek-flash

### Provider / routing chain

deepseek

### Additional provider/model setup details

_No response_

### Logs

```shell

```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

1. The stall happens between two plugin load steps

With `context-mode` enabled (all timestamps +08:00):

```
22:58:37.081 [plugins] codex failed during load ... (unrelated missing arm64 file; fails fast)
23:01:27.628 [context-mode]                         <-- first log line from context-mode register()
23:01:43.821 http server listening (3 plugins: context-mode, device-pair, memory-core; 203.4s)
```

There is a **170.5s gap** between the previous plugin's failure and the first
context-mode log line. After that point, startup finishes in ~16s.

Without `context-mode`:

```
22:00:29.517 [plugins] codex failed during load ...
22:00:45.434 [plugins] llama-cpp failed during load ...
22:00:45.478 http server listening (2 plugins: device-pair, memory-core; 31.4s)
```

No multi-minute gap.

### 2. The plugin's own `register()` is fast

Temporary `appendFileSync` timestamps were added to the plugin entry:

```
23:01:27.596 module-eval-done   (first line after static imports)
23:01:27.598 register-enter
23:01:27.660 register-exit      -> register() took ~62-65ms
```

The ~170s is spent **before** `module-eval-done`, i.e. in OpenClaw's module
resolution/capture/transformation path, not in plugin logic.

### 3. The same work done outside the gateway is much faster

On the same machine and files:

- `require(plugin.js)`: ~33ms
- jiti import of the plugin entry: ~27ms
- `capturePluginGenerationArtifact(...)` standalone: ~13.1s
- hashing/copying the plugin dependency tree (52MB / ~5.2k files): <5s

So the gateway-context load path is roughly 13x slower than the standalone capture
and appears to be the bottleneck.

### 4. Liveness confirms the ~165s stall

```
liveness heartbeat delayed: overdue=164177ms elapsed=194177ms; deferring recovery decisions
```

## Ruled out

- `fd`/`ripgrep` downloads: an earlier run did hit a 120s timeout downloading
  `fd-v10.5.0-aarch64...tar.gz`. After installing `fd-find`/`ripgrep` and removing
  the stale staging directory, startup still took ~203s. So the helper download is
  not the cause of this issue.
- Plugin code: `register()` is ~65ms; module import is ~27-33ms outside the gateway.
- Session/context-mode DB: constructor + cleanup + `ensureSession` measured at
  ~8ms / <1ms / <1ms in isolation.

### Impact and severity

_No response_

### Additional information

Hypothesis

OpenClaw's external-plugin generation/source-capture path
(`plugin-generation-artifact` / `plugin-source-capture`) is doing ~170s of work
before evaluating the plugin entry on this ARM64/PRoot filesystem. Possible causes:
repeated per-module capture/fingerprinting, or a long lock/timeout in the load path
that is amplified by PRoot's ptrace-based syscall interception.

## Requested

- Confirm whether `plugins.gateway-load.plugin.context-mode` reports `loadMs` around
  170s when `OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_STARTUP_TRACE=1` is enabled.
- Guidance or a workaround to avoid the slow capture path for an already-built
  external plugin (e.g. prefer prebuilt artifact / native load), or a fix in the
  loader.
- I am willing to test patches or run additional instrumentation.

## Workaround (current)

Keep `context-mode` disabled; the gateway then starts in ~10-30s.

## Trace collection (for maintainers)

Enable the gateway startup trace and restart:

```
OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_STARTUP_TRACE=1
```

Then look for `plugins.gateway-load.plugin.context-mode` metrics (`loadMs`,
`registerMs`, `loadAndRegisterMs`) in the gateway log.

issues.body:
## Summary

Every new session starts with 20-30% of context already consumed by bootstrap files (MEMORY.md ~1500-2000 tokens, plus SOUL.md, USER.md, AGENTS.md, IDENTITY.md, TOOLS.md, HEARTBEAT.md, BOOTSTRAP.md). On multi-turn conversations, these files are re-injected on every follow-up message, compounding the waste.

## The Problem

Today's bootstrap injection behavior:

1. Session start: All 8 bootstrap files injected into context (~15-20k tokens)
2. Every follow-up message: Bootstrap files re-injected again, duplicating content already in context
3. MEMORY.md is the worst offender: 1500-2000 tokens of mostly-stable data that rarely changes intra-session but gets re-loaded constantly

Result: Before the user even asks anything meaningful, 20-30% of a 200k context window is consumed by duplicate content.

## Existing Fixes Already Built (Not Enabled by Default)

OpenClaw already has the mechanics to fix this. They just aren't enabled:

### Fix 1: contextInjection: "continuation-skip" (one config line)

```json
{ "agents": { "defaults": { "contextInjection": "continuation-skip" } } }
```

This setting already exists in the codebase. It prevents bootstrap files from being re-injected after the first assistant reply. On a 10-message conversation, this saves ~9 re-injections of the full bootstrap payload.

Impact: 30-40% token reduction on multi-turn conversations. Zero breaking changes.

### Fix 2: MEMORY.md lazy-loading (default stub + on-demand load)

Replace the full MEMORY.md at session start with a thin stub:

```markdown
# MEMORY.md
Last updated: 2026-04-15
Summary: [2-3 line abstract]
Full content: memory_get("MEMORY.md")
```

The memory_search / memory_get tools already load memory content on-demand. The bootstrap file just needs to be small enough to not bloat context.

Impact: Saves ~1500-2000 tokens at every session start. Agents can still access full memory via existing tools.

### Fix 3: bootstrapDynamicFiles config (Issue #65438)

Mark frequently-changing workspace files as dynamic so they go after the OPENCLAW_CACHE_BOUNDARY. Currently only HEARTBEAT.md is dynamic. This would let users designate MEMORY.md and other volatile files to not invalidate prompt cache on every edit.

See: Issue #65438

## Proposed Solution

1. Enable contextInjection: "continuation-skip" by default - it already exists, just needs to be the default behavior
2. Use MEMORY.md stub by default - or at minimum, add a warning in docs about token cost of full MEMORY.md
3. Ship bootstrapDynamicFiles config - enables per-file cache boundary control (Issue #65438)

## Impact

For a typical user running 10 sessions/day with 10 messages each:
- Current: ~200k tokens/day wasted on duplicate bootstrap injection
- With fixes: ~60k tokens/day, same functionality
- At MiniMax pricing ($0.30/1M input): ~$0.05 saved/day per user
- At scale (1000 users): ~$18k/year in unnecessary API costs

More importantly: the 20-30% context overhead makes it harder to run efficient long conversations and pushes users toward expensive long-context models unnecessarily.

## References

- Issue #25369 (bootstrap re-read via tool calls - closed stale, same root cause)
- Issue #65438 (bootstrapDynamicFiles config - OPEN, related follow-up)

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

Summary
OpenClaw 2026.9.6 on macOS repeatedly closes agent database execution admission with:
StateDatabaseCoordinatorContentionError: another OpenClaw process owns state-lifecycle
However, read-only inspection of the state_leases table shows the active gateway-owner lease belongs to the same running Gateway process.
Environment
- OpenClaw: 2026.9.6
- macOS arm64
- Node.js: 24.19.0
- Gateway managed by launchd
- Gateway PID: 48500
- Gateway port: 18789
Verified ownership
state_leases.payload_json reports:
pid: 48500
host: Mac-mini.local
mode: supervised
supervisor.kind: launchd
supervisor.name: ai.openclaw.gateway
openclaw gateway status --deep independently reports:
Runtime: running (pid 48500, state active)
Listening: 127.0.0.1:18789
lsof shows the same Gateway process holding the shared and agent SQLite databases.
Actual behavior
Despite the Gateway being the valid lifecycle owner, OpenClaw intermittently produces:
- Agent database execution admission is closed
- another OpenClaw process owns state-lifecycle
- shared-state WAL maintenance failures
- idle shared-state cleanup failures
- memory sync failures
- Gateway HTTP request-handler failures
The errors continue after Gateway restart.
Expected behavior
Internal Gateway workers should recognize the current Gateway’s valid lifecycle lease and should not close agent execution admission as though a second OpenClaw process owned the state.
Impact
- Arc and specialist agents intermittently fail
- delegated work cannot start
- memory sync can fail
- Slack durability writes can fail
- multi-agent workflows are interrupted
Reproduction
1. Run OpenClaw 2026.9.6 under the normal launchd Gateway service.
2. Use multiple agents normally through the same Gateway.
3. Observe intermittent StateDatabaseCoordinatorContentionError.
4. Inspect state_leases.
5. Confirm the lease owner PID matches the currently running Gateway PID.
6. Observe continued contention errors after restart.
Diagnostic evidence
I have a sanitized openclaw triage diagnostic ZIP generated by OpenClaw and can attach it.
Triage was run read-only and no repair agent was started.

### Steps to reproduce

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Expected behavior

Prior to the 2026.9.6 update, this same single-Gateway multi-agent setup operated without closing agent database execution admission during normal concurrent agent work.

The running Gateway should recognize its own valid state-lifecycle ownership and allow its internal workers and agents to access the shared/agent SQLite databases normally.

A Gateway that owns the active gateway-owner lease should not treat that lease as belonging to “another OpenClaw process.”

### Actual behavior

On OpenClaw 2026.9.6, the running Gateway intermittently reports:

StateDatabaseCoordinatorContentionError: another OpenClaw process owns state-lifecycle

and:

Agent database execution admission is closed

This interrupts Arc and specialist-agent work, memory sync, Slack durability writes, database cleanup, WAL maintenance, and some Gateway HTTP requests.

Read-only inspection of state_leases shows the active gateway-owner lease belongs to PID 48500, supervised by launchd as ai.openclaw.gateway.

openclaw gateway status --deep independently confirms:

Runtime: running (pid 48500, state active)
Listening: 127.0.0.1:18789

lsof also showed the same Gateway process as the process holding the OpenClaw SQLite databases.

Despite this, the same running installation continues to report that “another OpenClaw process owns state-lifecycle.”

### OpenClaw version

2026.9.6 (eb377ac)

### Operating system

macOS 26.6.2 (arm64)

npm

openai/gpt-5.6-sol

OpenClaw Gateway -> OpenAI -> openai/gpt-5.6-sol

issues.body:
### Bug type

Crash (process/app exits or hangs)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

A managed npm upgrade from 2026.10.4 to 2026.10.5 installed the candidate but left the reserved `openclaw` system-agent database at schema 24 under an existing deletion-recovery hold. Doctor skipped that database, while Gateway startup still opened it and exited because 2026.10.5 requires schema 25. The documented `update repair` / `doctor --fix` recovery did not reconcile this mismatch.

### Steps to reproduce

Observed on one existing installation on October 19, 2026 (Asia/Shanghai), not a clean-install minimal reproducer:

1. Start with a working 2026.10.4 npm-global installation and a launchd-managed Gateway. The state contains the reserved `openclaw` database at schema 24 and a pre-existing recovery receipt:

   ```json
   {
     "source_key": "agent-deletion-journal-reconstruction",
     "status": "completed",
     "report": {
       "description": "Quarantined unusable agent deletion records; stores remain held for explicit recovery.",
       "held": [
         {
           "agentId": "openclaw",
           "path": "agents/openclaw/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite"
         }
       ]
     }
   }
   ```

   This is a projection of the stored receipt: `report` above represents the parsed `report_json` field, not a verbatim database row. The deletion journal itself has no remaining rows.

2. Trigger the managed stable-channel upgrade to 2026.10.5. Candidate admission, candidate Doctor/lint, configuration, plugins, recovery, and candidate Gateway startup pass.
3. Activation installs 2026.10.5, but its Doctor reports an offline-maintenance authority failure. The updater records `state-migrated-no-rollback`: `main` has migrated to schema 25, while the held system-agent database remains at 24.
4. From an independent terminal, run `openclaw update repair --yes --json`, then `openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive`.
5. Repair converges the `zai` plugin to 2026.10.5. Doctor still leaves the reserved system-agent store held and unmigrated. The managed Gateway starts repeatedly, then exits during session admission with the schema mismatch.

No production upgrade replay was performed. An isolated-copy migration check was performed during recovery, described below.

### Expected behavior

Doctor's own guidance says held stores remain untouched and updates can continue. That requires the updater, migration admission, and runtime startup to agree on the disposition of the reserved helper.

If the helper is required at runtime, provide a supported, ownership-verified reconciliation/migration path for its existing recovery hold. If it is intentionally retained and ineligible, runtime should not reopen it as an active current-schema dependency. Preserve genuine deletion fences and held data; do not migrate or activate all held stores indiscriminately.

### Actual behavior

Sanitized excerpts from the update record, Doctor output, and Gateway log:

```text
before: 2026.10.4
after: 2026.10.5
reason: state-migrated-no-rollback

Doctor config promotion refused for top-level keys: none recorded.
authority-check-failed:
OpenClaw state at <state>/state/openclaw.sqlite is undergoing offline maintenance; retry when it finishes.

Held agent openclaw database <state>/agents/openclaw/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite
(deletion journal reconstructed); run openclaw doctor --fix to inspect restoration.

openclaw is a reserved system agent and cannot be added or deleted.
Its store remains untouched; review its deletion recovery receipt, then run openclaw doctor --fix.

Gateway migration recovery did not finish:
<state>/agents/openclaw/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite: expected schema 25, found 24.

Gateway failed to start:
OpenClaw agent database <state>/agents/openclaw/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite
uses schema version 24; stop active agents and run openclaw doctor --fix
to migrate session identities before using it.
```

Independent launchd inspection showed repeated exits with code 78 and no listener. After the startup failures, the restart-loop breaker also suppressed Telegram auto-start.

The identity of the process holding the original offline-maintenance window was not established. This report does not claim that the hold mismatch caused that first authority failure; the subsequent schema-related startup failures were directly observed.

### OpenClaw version

Driver/source: 2026.10.4, build `2026.10.4-release-383c124cc32f-2026-10-15T17-18-22.749Z`.

Installed candidate and repaired runtime: 2026.10.5 (`1b58cb9`), build `2026.10.5-release-1b58cb9a1b4f-2026-10-18T17-23-40.943Z`.

### Operating system

macOS 27.0.1, arm64; Node v26.11.1; npm 11.20.0.

### Install method

Homebrew-prefix npm-global package; native managed update initiated from chat; launchd LaunchAgent Gateway.

### Model

Not applicable: failure occurs during local migration and Gateway startup, before inference.

### Provider / routing chain

Not applicable to this failure boundary.

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Read-only inspection of the installed 2026.10.5 implementation found:

- `createAgentDatabaseDeletionClassifier` classifies the system-agent path as `held`. Calling the packaged classifier against the live state after recovery still returns `held`; `main` is active.
- `openclaw-database-preflight` excludes held paths from maintenance candidates, while its runtime candidate filter does not exclude the string-valued `held` classification.
- `repairDoctorAgentDeletionJournal` leaves this existing hold in place. Its reserved-ID branch says the system agent cannot be added/deleted and recommends Doctor again.
- The Gateway log directly shows the held database being opened at startup and rejected for schema 24.

These are installed-release observations, not a current-main reproduction or a claim about unreleased fixes.

### Impact and severity

One observed upgrade left the managed Gateway unavailable. Native repair fixed plugin convergence and updated the service shutdown budget, but did not resolve the system-agent schema mismatch. Repeated boot failures additionally disabled channel auto-start. No data loss was observed; recurrence frequency beyond this incident is unknown.

### Additional information

Recovery was diagnostic, not a supported CLI-only solution:

- Preserved the existing update recovery artifacts and made consistent SQLite backups. All three databases passed integrity checks.
- With the affected service stopped, validated the installed candidate's `migrateOpenClawAgentDatabaseForMaintenance` on an isolated copy, under its native Doctor maintenance lock and agent-database maintenance lease.
- Applied the same narrowly scoped migration to the original reserved system-agent database, from schema 24 to 25. No schema-number-only SQL edit, database deletion, or package source patch was made. The system-agent database had zero session/transcript rows before and after migration.
- Started the Gateway and manually resumed the suppressed Telegram channel. Gateway version is 2026.10.5, `/readyz` returns HTTP 200, Telegram is connected and its API probe passes, and main-agent session/transcript counts match the backup.
- The existing `held` receipt remains. A future schema bump could encounter the same mismatch if its eligibility is not reconciled; that is a risk inferred from the retained state and installed code, not an executed future-upgrade test.

Related reports checked before filing:

- #164316 / #165215: closed deletion-journal recovery reports. The preserved reserved-agent hold still matters when a later release changes its schema. This is fresh 2026.10.4 -> 2026.10.5 field evidence.
- #172740, closed by #172975: post-activation verification rejected intentionally retained deleted-agent schemas during a Git update. This incident concerns an npm update and a reserved system-agent store that the live Gateway actually reopens.
- #164799 / #176355: reserved system-agent startup preparation refuses a missing configured target. Our observed fatal error is schema 24 versus 25, not `database configuration changed during startup inspection`.

Please provide a supported recovery path and a regression check covering a reserved system-agent recovery hold across a schema-changing upgrade, including the installed driver's recovery and live Gateway startup.

No private configuration, credentials, account/host identifiers, chat content, raw logs, database files, or diagnostic archives are attached.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

A skill whose `requires.bins` names a binary is reported as eligible and model-visible by `openclaw skills check` when a directory with that binary's name sits on `PATH`, even though no executable with that name exists.

### Steps to reproduce

All paths below are placeholders. `<fixture>` is an empty scratch directory and the state directory is isolated and empty at the start. No Gateway is running.

1. Create a `PATH` entry that holds a directory named like the binary, and a workspace skill that requires it:

   ```bash
   mkdir -p <fixture>/bin/fixture-gog-tool        # a directory, not an executable
   mkdir -p <fixture>/workspace/skills/fixture-gog-skill
   cat > <fixture>/workspace/skills/fixture-gog-skill/SKILL.md <<'SKILL'
   ---
   name: fixture-gog-skill
   description: Fixture skill requiring an external binary
   metadata: { "openclaw": { "requires": { "bins": ["fixture-gog-tool"] } } }
   ---

   Fixture body.
   SKILL
   command -v fixture-gog-tool                     # prints nothing: no executable of that name
   ```

2. Point an isolated config at that workspace:

   ```bash
   mkdir -p <fixture>/state
   cat > <fixture>/state/openclaw.json <<'CONF'
   { "agents": { "defaults": { "workspace": "<fixture>/workspace" } } }
   CONF
   ```

3. Ask the CLI which skills are usable:

   ```bash
   OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH=<fixture>/state/openclaw.json \
   OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=<fixture>/state \
   OPENCLAW_HOME=<fixture>/home \
   PATH=<fixture>/bin:$PATH \
   openclaw skills check --json
   ```

4. Remove the directory and run the same command again as a control:

   ```bash
   rmdir <fixture>/bin/fixture-gog-tool
   ```

### Expected behavior

Both runs report the same thing, because in neither case is there an executable named `fixture-gog-tool`: `fixture-gog-skill` is absent from `eligible`, `modelVisible` and `commandVisible`, and has an entry under `missingRequirements` with `"bins": ["fixture-gog-tool"]`. That is exactly what the control run in step 4 produces.

### Actual behavior

With the directory present, the skill is reported ready and is offered to the agent. Excerpts from `skills check --json`, filtered to the fixture skill:

```
eligible       contains fixture-gog-skill: yes
modelVisible   contains fixture-gog-skill: yes
commandVisible contains fixture-gog-skill: yes
missingRequirements entry for fixture-gog-skill: none
```

After `rmdir` of that same directory, with nothing else changed:

```
eligible       contains fixture-gog-skill: no
modelVisible   contains fixture-gog-skill: no
commandVisible contains fixture-gog-skill: no
missingRequirements entry for fixture-gog-skill:
  { "name": "fixture-gog-skill",
    "missing": { "bins": ["fixture-gog-tool"], "anyBins": [], "env": [], "config": [], "os": [] },
    "install": [] }
```

The other skills in the report are identical between the two runs. The presence of the directory alone flips the availability answer for the skill that requires that binary, so the skill is injected and offered to the model and fails only when it actually tries to run the binary.

### OpenClaw version

2026.9.4 (source checkout at 7a92d3633b9)

### Operating system

Ubuntu 22.04 (Linux kernel 6.8), Node.js v24

### Install method

Source checkout, run through the repository CLI wrapper

### Model

Not applicable. `openclaw skills check` reports requirement state locally and does not call a model.

### Provider / routing chain

Not applicable. Local CLI only, no Gateway and no provider requests.

### Additional provider/model setup details

None. The only config is the isolated state directory and the fixture workspace skill above.

### Logs

```shell
$ ls -la <fixture>/bin
drwxrwxr-x 2 user user 4096 fixture-gog-tool      # a directory
$ command -v fixture-gog-tool
(prints nothing)

# WITH the directory on PATH
$ openclaw skills check --json
  eligible       contains fixture-gog-skill: yes
  modelVisible   contains fixture-gog-skill: yes
  commandVisible contains fixture-gog-skill: yes
  missingRequirements entry for fixture-gog-skill: none

# control: same command after `rmdir <fixture>/bin/fixture-gog-tool`
$ openclaw skills check --json
  eligible       contains fixture-gog-skill: no
  modelVisible   contains fixture-gog-skill: no
  commandVisible contains fixture-gog-skill: no
  missingRequirements entry for fixture-gog-skill:
    {"name": "fixture-gog-skill",
     "missing": {"bins": ["fixture-gog-tool"], "anyBins": [], "env": [], "config": [], "os": []},
     "install": []}
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Terminal output only. The output above is from the reproduction, with local paths replaced by `<fixture>`.

### Impact and severity

- Affected: operators whose `PATH` contains a directory named exactly like a binary a skill or hook requires. A plausible source is a tool checkout directory placed on `PATH`, or a `PATH` entry that is itself a per-tool directory tree.
- Severity: blocks the workflow the requirement check exists to protect. The requirement gate that should hide an unusable skill stays silent, and the skill is handed to the agent.
- Frequency: always, in the reproduction 1/1 with the directory present and 1/1 correct with it absent.
- Consequence: the agent is told a capability is available and only discovers otherwise when the tool invocation fails. The answer is also cached for as long as `PATH` and `PATHEXT` stay unchanged, so it does not self-correct within the process.

### Additional information

The same availability probe (`hasBinary` in `src/shared/config-eval.ts`) is read by hook eligibility and status (`src/hooks/config.ts`, `src/hooks/hooks-status.ts`), the Gmail watcher start check (`src/hooks/gmail-watcher.ts`, which otherwise reports `gog binary not found`), Gmail setup steps, and the `brew` / `uv` / `go` / `apt-get` prerequisite checks in skill installation (`src/skills/lifecycle/install.ts`). Those paths were read in source and not separately exercised in this report.

The repository's executable-resolution owner already rejects this case: `isExecutableFile` in `src/infra/executable-path.ts` begins with `if (!isRegularFile(filePath)) return false;`. The same directory-as-executable mistake was fixed recently in adjacent code by https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/144681.

issues.body:
## Summary `openclaw --profile

gateway install` run from inside a Gateway-hosted exec (where the host Gateway's secret egress proxy is enabled) writes the caller's process-owned `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` value into the generated systemd user unit as `Environment=NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/secret-egress-proxy/gateway-/trust-bundle.pem`. That bundle belongs to the *calling* Gateway's process lifetime (the docs say the CA is generated per Gateway start). After that Gateway restarts the directory is gone, so every process of the installed Gateway logs at start: `Warning: Ignoring extra certs from `.../secret-egress-proxy/gateway-XXXX/trust-bundle.pem`, load failed: ... No such file or directory` and all of its children (MCP stdio servers, codex app-server, onnx host) inherit the stale path. While the other Gateway is still up, the installed Gateway would trust another profile's ephemeral proxy CA. ## Environment - OpenClaw 2026.10.4 (383c124), Linux (Ubuntu, systemd user service) - Two profiles on one host; second profile installed from an exec of the first, with `secrets.egressProxy.enabled: true` on the first. ## Repro 1. Gateway A with `secrets.egressProxy.enabled: true`. 2. From a Gateway-hosted exec on A: `openclaw --profile b gateway install`. 3. `grep NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS ~/.config/systemd/user/openclaw-gateway-b.service` → path under A's state dir. 4. Restart A; start B → "Ignoring extra certs" warning in B's journal; `/proc//environ` of B and its children carries A's stale path. ## Expected The service environment snapshot should exclude egress-proxy-injected variables (`NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` / proxy vars that point at a `secret-egress-proxy` directory), the same way it already avoids other per-process Gateway variables.

issues.body:
### Summary
`openclaw wiki ingest` (CLI) fails with `Memory Wiki vault changed while its compiled cache was being built.` whenever a gateway-side `wiki.bridge.import` for the same agent vault runs at the same time. The ingest has already written its source page and logged the `ingest` event; only the trailing auto-compile throws, so the command exits 1 for work that actually landed.

### Version / platform
OpenClaw 2026.10.4, Linux (Ubuntu, x64), Node 26. memory-wiki config: `vault.scope: agent`, `vaultMode: bridge`, `bridge.enabled: true`, `ingest.autoCompile: true`. Agent vault holds ~6,240 source pages, so a compile takes ~85 s.

### Root cause (from dist code)
- `withMemoryWikiVaultMutation()` serialises vault mutations with an **in-process** keyed queue (`vaultMutationQueue` + AsyncLocalStorage). There is no cross-process lock.
- The CLI `wiki ingest` action calls `ingestMemoryWikiSource()` **locally** in the CLI process (it never routes to the gateway's existing `wiki.ingest` method), and `ingestMemoryWikiSource()` always ends with `compileMemoryWikiVault()`.
- `wiki.bridge.import` (and the background `syncImportedSourcesInBackground`) runs in the **gateway** process and rewrites `sources/bridge-*.md`.
- The compile computes `resolveMemoryWikiVaultSourceGeneration()` (sha256 over `sources/entities/concepts/syntheses/reports`) before and after the scan; the gateway's writes change it mid-scan, so `compileMemoryWikiVaultUnlocked` throws. Nothing retries.

### Evidence (timestamps from `.openclaw-wiki/log.jsonl` and the gateway journal, 2026-10-18 UTC)
- 23:35:00.866 `ingest` sources/fact-annotation-proposals-pending-superseded-by-note-edits.md (CLI) → 23:35:00.956 compile reservation
- 23:35:06.276 bridge import event (updatedCount 3, removedCount 1) → 23:35:06.403 second compile reservation
- gateway: `wiki.bridge.import 149699ms` completed 23:37:31 (started ~23:35:02)
- CLI ingest exits 1 after ~85 s with "Memory Wiki vault changed while its compiled cache was being built."; the page itself was written.
Reproduced by hand at 23:36 UTC: `openclaw wiki --agent main ingest <existing page source> --json`, started while that `wiki.bridge.import` was still in flight, exited 1 after 85 s with the same message. Our scheduled ingesting job hit this whenever its ingests overlapped our :05/:35 bridge-import schedule (earlier failures that day were a separate SQLite lock-contention problem).

### Expected
Either (a) a cross-process vault mutation lock (file lock under `.openclaw-wiki/`) so CLI and gateway writers serialise, (b) CLI `wiki ingest` routing through the gateway's `wiki.ingest` when the gateway is reachable (as `wiki bridge import` / `wiki status` already do), or (c) the compile retrying/rebasing when the source generation moves, with ingest not reporting failure after its write succeeded.

### Workaround
Schedule CLI ingests outside the bridge-import window. Related but distinct: #168793, #168784 (compiled-cache row lifecycle).

issues.body:
## Summary

In a long-running Telegram direct conversation used to manage several parallel projects, context compaction omitted one active project (**Avenbot**) from the compacted summary. The session itself continued, but when the user later asked the agent to list the projects discussed, Avenbot was missing.

The normal recovery path also failed: repeated calls to `agent_knowledge_recall` returned only:

```
recall failed: {"error":"Upstream Hindsight request failed."}
```

This combination makes a single long-lived personal agent unreliable for managing multiple project streams: a fact dropped by compaction becomes unrecoverable unless the user repeats it manually.

## Environment

- OpenClaw: `2026.7.1`
- Channel: Telegram direct conversation
- Conversation shape: long-lived, tool-heavy session with several parallel project streams
- Memory/recall path: Hindsight-backed `agent_knowledge_recall`

No Telegram IDs, credentials, raw chat text, or user-specific configuration are included here.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Use one Telegram agent session for several independent, ongoing projects.
2. Let the conversation grow until automatic compaction occurs.
3. Have one active project mentioned in older conversation history but not promoted into the workspace `MEMORY.md`.
4. After compaction, ask the agent to enumerate the projects discussed.
5. Observe that one active project is absent from the compacted summary.
6. Try to recover it with `agent_knowledge_recall`.
7. Repeat the recall on later turns.

## Actual behavior

- The post-compaction session remains usable, so this is not a complete session reset.
- The compacted summary omits an active project.
- `agent_knowledge_recall` fails repeatedly with the generic upstream Hindsight error.
- Workspace memory contains other projects but cannot restore the omitted one.
- The assistant has to ask the user to repeat information that was already provided.

The recall failure was observed repeatedly across separate turns rather than as a single transient call.

## Expected behavior

At least one recovery layer should preserve continuity:

1. Pre-compaction memory flush should retain active project/entity names and their current status; or
2. Hindsight recall should retrieve facts from pre-compaction history; or
3. If Hindsight is temporarily unavailable, OpenClaw should fall back to searching the prior session transcript / last valid checkpoint; or
4. The error should expose an actionable status and correlation information instead of only `Upstream Hindsight request failed`.

A useful invariant would be: after compaction, every active project present before compaction is either represented in the compacted summary, promoted to durable memory, or retrievable through recall.

## Impact

For personal agents that coordinate multiple workstreams, this appears to the user as selective amnesia. It undermines the core expectation that one bot can maintain several concurrent projects.

## Related issue

- #60213 describes total session loss/orphaning after compaction. This report is different: the session continued, but compaction was lossy and the memory fallback failed, producing selective unrecoverable loss.

## Suggested diagnostics/tests

- Add an integration test with multiple named active workstreams across a compaction boundary.
- Simulate a Hindsight outage during post-compaction recall and verify transcript/checkpoint fallback.
- Log a non-sensitive failure category/correlation ID for Hindsight upstream errors.
- Verify that pre-compaction flush captures active entities/workstreams, not only recently repeated facts.
